label: Mnemonics
description: Front: just the mnemonic phrase. Back: full unpacking with each part explained, why it matters, and examples. The 'what to chant on the way to the exam' deck.

cards.term: Populations Pivot, Individuals Don't
cards.definition:
🧬 WHAT EVOLUTION IS

📌 The phrase: Evolution = change in allele frequencies across generations within a population. Individuals develop; populations evolve.

◆ POPULATIONS PIVOT — allele/genotype frequencies shift over generations. This is the unit of evolution.
◆ INDIVIDUALS DON'T — an individual's DNA does not 'evolve' during its lifetime. It develops, ages, dies — but its alleles don't change in response to selection.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: This is the cleanest one-line correction to the common error 'a giraffe stretched its neck to evolve a longer one.' Evolution is a population statistic, not an individual achievement.

⚠ TRAP: 'Lamarckian' thinking — assuming that traits acquired during life pass to offspring. They don't (with rare epigenetic exceptions); only allele changes in the germline transmit.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#17] Which of the following best defines biological evolution?
  A. An individual organism becoming better adapted over its lifetime.
  B. Change in the heritable traits of a population across generations.
  C. Progressive improvement of organisms toward greater complexity.
  D. Random variation among individuals within a single generation.
→ Answer: B

[Final-A · MC#7] In which scenario does NATURAL SELECTION OCCUR but NO EVOLUTION result?
  A. A population shows heritable variation in beak depth, and large-beaked birds reproduce more during a drought.
  B. Two populations are separated by a mountain range and experience different selective pressures.
  C. A herd of cattle has variation in milk yield due entirely to feed differences (h² = 0)
  D. Bacteria exposed to antibiotics develop resistance through mutation.
→ Answer: C

cards.term: Mutation Makes, Selection Sorts, Drift Drifts, Flow Flows
cards.definition:
🧬 THE 4 MECHANISMS OF EVOLUTION

📌 The phrase: Every observed change in allele frequency is caused by one (or a combination) of these four processes. There are no others.

◆ MUTATION MAKES — the ONLY source of new genetic variation. Random with respect to fitness. Includes synonymous, missense, nonsense, frameshift, and structural changes.
◆ SELECTION SORTS — non-random differential survival/reproduction based on phenotype. The ONLY mechanism that produces adaptation.
◆ DRIFT DRIFTS — random sampling error from generation to generation. Strong in small populations (bottlenecks, founder effects); negligible in huge ones.
◆ FLOW FLOWS — gene flow / migration. Moves alleles between populations. Homogenizes populations and opposes local adaptation.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: This single phrase is the ENTIRE skeleton of evolutionary genetics. Memorize this and you can classify any case study.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Sickle-cell allele frequency in West Africa is high because SELECTION favors AS heterozygotes in malaria zones. Modern frequency varies by region because of GENE FLOW from migration, MUTATION created the original allele, and DRIFT shapes small isolated communities.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#9] Hospitals that heavily use a particular antibiotic see rising rates of resistance to that antibiotic. Which evolutionary mechanism is most directly responsible?
  A. Natural selection on rare resistant mutants that arise independently of the antibiotic.
  B. Lamarckian inheritance — bacteria acquire resistance from exposure and pass it to offspring.
  C. Mutation rate increases when antibiotics are present, generating resistance on demand.
  D. Genetic drift — random change in a small bacterial population.
→ Answer: A

[Final-D · MC#5] Antibiotic resistance in bacteria is a textbook example of natural selection because:
  A. Resistance is acquired during a bacterium's lifetime and passed via cell division.
  B. Antibiotics induce mutations toward resistance.
  C. Resistance mutations occur randomly
  D. Bacteria deliberately evolve resistance.
→ Answer: C

cards.term: V-H-D-F: Variation, Heritable, Differential, Fitness
cards.definition:
🎯 DARWIN'S 4 REQUIREMENTS FOR NATURAL SELECTION

📌 The phrase: For natural selection to operate, ALL FOUR must be true. Miss any one and there's no evolution by selection.

◆ V — VARIATION exists in the trait among individuals
◆ H — HERITABLE: at least some of that variation has a genetic basis (h² > 0)
◆ D — DIFFERENTIAL survival/reproduction: individuals with different traits leave different numbers of offspring
◆ F — FITNESS-related: the trait must affect lifetime reproductive success

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: This is the deductive logic of natural selection. If a question asks 'why isn't selection acting on X?' — check which letter fails.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Eye color in humans varies (V), is heritable (H), and people differ in offspring count (D) — but eye color doesn't affect reproduction (no F). So no selection on eye color.

⚠ TRAP: Selection ≠ evolution. Selection acts every generation, but unless trait is HERITABLE (H), allele frequencies don't change.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#16] All three of the following must be present for natural selection to produce evolution. Which is NOT required?
  A. Differential survival or reproduction associated with the trait.
  B. The trait must be heritable — required
  C. Variation in a trait among individuals in the population.
  D. The trait must benefit the species as a whole.
→ Answer: D

[Final-A · MC#7] In which scenario does NATURAL SELECTION OCCUR but NO EVOLUTION result?
  A. A population shows heritable variation in beak depth, and large-beaked birds reproduce more during a drought.
  B. Two populations are separated by a mountain range and experience different selective pressures.
  C. A herd of cattle has variation in milk yield due entirely to feed differences (h² = 0)
  D. Bacteria exposed to antibiotics develop resistance through mutation.
→ Answer: C

cards.term: Hutton-Lyell built TIME, Smith stacked LAYERS, Cuvier confirmed DEATH, Lamarck guessed CHANGE, Darwin & Wallace cracked HOW
cards.definition:
📜 PRE-DARWINIAN HISTORY OF EVOLUTIONARY THOUGHT

📌 The phrase: 5 contributions that built the foundation Darwin walked into. Each one removed a different obstacle to the theory.

◆ HUTTON & LYELL (Uniformitarianism) — 'TIME': same slow processes shaping the Earth today shaped the past. Gave Darwin the deep time he needed for slow gradual change.
◆ WILLIAM SMITH (Stratigraphy) — 'LAYERS': same fossils appear in same rock layers worldwide; index fossils mark age. Showed the fossil record is ordered.
◆ CUVIER (Comparative anatomy) — 'DEATH': mammoths ≠ living elephants; species can go extinct. If species can DIE, the world isn't fixed.
◆ LAMARCK (Inheritance of acquired traits) — 'CHANGE': wrong mechanism, but right that species transform over time. The giraffe's neck argument.
◆ DARWIN & WALLACE (1858 joint paper, Origin 1859) — 'HOW': natural selection. The mechanism that ties it all together.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Darwin didn't invent evolution from scratch. Knowing the build-up tells you exactly what his contribution was — the MECHANISM (selection), not the IDEA of change.

📖 STORY: Wallace sent Darwin a manuscript from the Malay Archipelago in 1858 with the same theory. Darwin had been sitting on the idea for 20 years and was forced to publish jointly.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#26] Whose work using fossils and stratigraphy helped establish extinction as a real phenomenon?
  A. William Smith
  B. Charles Darwin
  C. Alfred Russel Wallace
  D. Jean-Baptiste Lamarck
→ Answer: A

[Final-D · MC#21] Which naturalist independently conceived natural selection and, by sending Darwin a letter outlining the idea in 1858, prompted Darwin to publish his work?
  A. Thomas Malthus
  B. Charles Lyell
  C. Alfred Russel Wallace
  D. Gregor Mendel
→ Answer: C

cards.term: Synonymous Silent, Missense Modifies, Nonsense Knocks-out, Frameshift Fries
cards.definition:
🧬 THE 4 OUTCOMES OF POINT/INDEL MUTATIONS

📌 The phrase: Listed from least to most disruptive effect on the protein.

◆ SYNONYMOUS SILENT — base change, but redundancy of the genetic code means same amino acid. No protein change. Often invisible to selection.
◆ MISSENSE MODIFIES — base change → different amino acid. Can be neutral, harmful, or beneficial. Sickle-cell HbS (Glu→Val) is a famous missense.
◆ NONSENSE KNOCKS-OUT — base change creates a premature stop codon → truncated, usually non-functional protein. Often catastrophic (Duchenne, etc.).
◆ FRAMESHIFT FRIES — insertion or deletion of bases not divisible by 3 → reading frame shifts → ENTIRE downstream sequence garbled. Almost always devastating.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Knowing the mutation type predicts the phenotypic effect — which predicts the strength of selection against it.

⚠ TRAP: Mutation is RANDOM with respect to fitness. None of these mutations 'try' to be silent or harmful — they happen, then selection sorts them.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#18] When biologists say mutations are 'random,' they specifically mean:
  A. Mutations only occur during environmental stress.
  B. Mutations are unpredictable and cannot be studied scientifically.
  C. Mutations occur at every base of the genome with equal probability.
  D. Mutations are not directed toward producing adaptations that the organism needs.
→ Answer: D

[Final-B · MC#23] Influenza virus rapidly evolves resistance to antiviral drugs. Which statement best captures the role of mutation in this process?
  A. Antiviral exposure causes the virus to mutate toward resistance.
  B. The drug induces directed mutations only in the genes that confer resistance.
  C. Mutations conferring resistance arise by chance independently of drug presence
  D. Resistance is acquired during the host's lifetime and passed to offspring viruses through epigenetic inheritance.
→ Answer: C

cards.term: Dom Decides alone, Rec Recedes, Add Averages
cards.definition:
🧬 ALLELE EFFECTS ON PHENOTYPE

📌 The phrase: Three ways a single allele can contribute to phenotype.

◆ DOM DECIDES ALONE — Dominant: one copy is enough to express the phenotype. Heterozygote (Aa) looks like homozygote (AA). Used by classic Mendelian dominance.
◆ REC RECEDES — Recessive: needs two copies (aa) to show. Hidden in heterozygotes. Most genetic diseases are recessive (cystic fibrosis, sickle-cell SS).
◆ ADD AVERAGES — Additive: each copy adds equally to phenotype. AA = 2 units; Aa = 1 unit; aa = 0 units. The genetic basis of quantitative/continuous traits and the source of V_A heritability.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Only ADDITIVE variance (V_A) reliably transmits to offspring — that's why narrow-sense h² (V_A/V_P) predicts response to selection, while broad-sense H² doesn't.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#1] If alleles at a locus act additively, the phenotype of an Aa heterozygote is most likely:
  A. Identical to AA homozygote.
  B. Wholly different from either homozygote.
  C. Identical to aa homozygote.
  D. Intermediate between AA and aa.
→ Answer: D

[Final-B · MC#9] In a population of 200 diploid individuals, the genotype counts are 50 AA, 100 Aa, and 50 aa. What is the frequency of allele A?
  A. 0.75
  B. 0.50
  C. 0.40
  D. 0.25
→ Answer: B

cards.term: 5 NOs: No Mutation, No Migration, No Selection, No Non-random mating, No drift
cards.definition:
⚖️ HARDY-WEINBERG ASSUMPTIONS

📌 The phrase: For a population to remain at HWE (genotype frequencies = p², 2pq, q²), all 5 must hold. Violation of ANY one shifts allele or genotype frequencies.

◆ NO MUTATION — alleles aren't being created or destroyed
◆ NO MIGRATION — no gene flow in or out
◆ NO SELECTION — all genotypes have equal fitness
◆ NO NON-RANDOM MATING — mates pair up by chance, not by phenotype/relatedness (no inbreeding, no assortative mating)
◆ NO DRIFT — population is effectively infinite (huge N)

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: HWE is the NULL hypothesis of population genetics. Real populations rarely meet it perfectly. Deviations REVEAL which mechanism is acting — that's how we discover evolution from data.

🧮 EQUATIONS: p + q = 1 · p² + 2pq + q² = 1 · 2pq = heterozygote frequency.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Disease aa frequency = 1/10,000 → q² = 0.0001 → q = 0.01 → p = 0.99 → carriers 2pq ≈ 0.02 (1 in 50). Far more carriers than affected.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#23] Which of the following is NOT one of the five assumptions of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
  A. Random mating
  B. Infinite population size
  C. Equal allele frequencies
  D. No mutation
→ Answer: C

[Final-C · MC#11] A population has p = 0.4 (allele A) and q = 0.6 (allele a). Hardy-Weinberg expects 32% heterozygotes (2pq = 0.48 → 48%, sorry let me recompute: 2 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 0.48 = 48%). The population is observed to have only 20% heterozygotes. Which mechanism best explains this deviation?
  A. Inbreeding or population subdivision
  B. Strong selection against the AA homozygote
  C. Heterozygote advantage (overdominance)
  D. Recent admixture between populations
→ Answer: A

cards.term: Big H is Whole-Genetic; small h is Additive-only
cards.definition:
📊 BROAD vs NARROW HERITABILITY

📌 The phrase: Two different heritability measures — be careful which one you mean.

◆ BIG H (broad-sense) = V_G / V_P — the proportion of phenotypic variance due to ALL genetic variance (additive + dominance + interaction)
◆ SMALL h (narrow-sense) = V_A / V_P — only the ADDITIVE genetic variance, the part that reliably transmits to offspring

📐 Variance partition:
V_P = V_G + V_E + V_GxE (phenotypic = genetic + environmental + interaction)
V_G = V_A + V_D + V_I (genetic = additive + dominance + epistatic)

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Only h² (small h) predicts the response to selection via the breeder's equation R = h²S. Dominance and epistatic effects don't transmit cleanly because they depend on which OTHER alleles a parent's gametes meet.

⚠ TRAP: Saying 'heritability is 80%' is meaningless without specifying broad vs narrow. Most ecological and breeder estimates are NARROW.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-C · MC#24] Which formula correctly defines narrow-sense heritability h²?
  A. h² = V_E / V_P
  B. h² = V_G / V_P
  C. h² = R · S
  D. h² = V_A / V_P
→ Answer: D

[Final-C · MC#2] Total phenotypic variance V_P can be partitioned as:
  A. V_P = h² + V_E
  B. V_P = V_A · V_E
  C. V_P = V_G + V_E
  D. V_P = V_A + V_D + V_I + V_E
→ Answer: D

cards.term: S says how hard you push, h² says how much it sticks
cards.definition:
📐 BREEDER'S EQUATION INTUITION

📌 The phrase: R = h² × S. Response equals heritability times selection differential.

◆ S (selection differential) = mean of selected parents minus population mean. 'How hard you push' — how strongly you favor extreme individuals.
◆ h² (narrow heritability) = V_A / V_P. 'How much it sticks' — what fraction of the parent shift transmits to offspring.
◆ R (response) = how much the offspring mean shifts compared to parent population. The actual evolutionary change.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: The most important equation in quantitative genetics. Used by every plant/animal breeder, ecologist measuring selection in the wild, and conservation geneticist predicting outcomes.

🔬 EXAMPLE: If chicken egg weight has h² = 0.4 and you select hens whose mean exceeds the flock by S = 5 g, expected response is R = 0.4 × 5 = 2 g per generation.

⚠ TRAP: If h² = 0, no response no matter how hard you select. Many traits look responsive at first but aren't truly heritable — they revert.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-B · MC#19] A trait has a large selection differential S but heritability h² = 0. What is the predicted response to selection R?
  A. Equal to S, since selection is strong.
  B. Negative — the population evolves the opposite way.
  C. Half of S, on average.
  D. R = 0, regardless of S.
→ Answer: D

[Final-B · MC#28] A breeder selects heifers with the highest milk yield (mean = 25 kg/day) from a herd with mean 20 kg/day, and breeds them. Heritability of milk yield is h² = 0.4. What is the predicted mean milk yield of the next generation?
  A. 25 kg/day
  B. 23 kg/day
  C. 20 kg/day (no change)
  D. 22 kg/day
→ Answer: D

cards.term: Stabilizing Squeezes the middle, Directional Drives one tail, Disruptive Divides into two
cards.definition:
🎯 THE 3 MODES OF NATURAL SELECTION

📌 The phrase: Each mode produces a different effect on a trait's distribution. The bell-curve shape tells you which one is acting.

◆ STABILIZING SQUEEZES — extremes punished, middle wins → variance SHRINKS, mean stays. Example: human birth weight (very small or very large babies have higher mortality).
◆ DIRECTIONAL DRIVES — one tail wins, mean SHIFTS in that direction. Example: Galápagos finches in 1977 drought — bigger beaks survived to crack hard seeds; mean beak depth shifted up.
◆ DISRUPTIVE DIVIDES — both extremes win, middle punished → variance INCREASES, can produce bimodal distribution. Can drive sympatric speciation. Example: African seedcrackers — small or huge beaks, no medium.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Predicts the EVOLUTIONARY TRAJECTORY. Stabilizing maintains status quo; directional drives change; disruptive can split a lineage.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Industrial melanism in peppered moths = directional. Variance in human birth weight in modern hospitals (still stabilizing, but weaker thanks to medicine).

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-B · MC#7] After the 1977 drought on Daphne Major, the medium ground finch population shifted toward deeper beaks. The Grants concluded this was natural selection because:
  A. The drought directly caused beaks to grow.
  B. All small-beaked birds happened to die randomly.
  C. Birds physically modified their beaks to deal with hard seeds.
  D. Beak depth was heritable
→ Answer: D

[Final-D · MC#19] Fisheries with minimum-size limits (only large fish kept, small ones returned) have led to evolution toward earlier maturation and smaller maximum size in many fish populations. Why?
  A. Fish randomly become smaller over time.
  B. Smaller fish have higher mutation rates.
  C. Younger fish have lower nutritional needs.
  D. Selection imposed by humans removes large individuals before they reproduce
→ Answer: D

cards.term: Negative-FD lets the rare win, Positive-FD piles on the common
cards.definition:
🎯 FREQUENCY-DEPENDENT SELECTION

📌 The phrase: Fitness depends on how COMMON your phenotype is in the population.

◆ NEGATIVE FD — rare phenotype has highest fitness; common phenotype has lowest. MAINTAINS diversity. Examples: side-blotched lizard rock-paper-scissors, MHC immune alleles, left/right-handed scale-eating fish.
◆ POSITIVE FD — common phenotype has highest fitness; rare punished. LOCKS IN one form. Examples: Müllerian mimicry warning colors (predators learn the common pattern), human language conventions.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Frequency-dependence is one of the few mechanisms that maintains polymorphism under selection — without it, selection usually FIXES the best allele. Explains why so many populations have multiple stable morphs.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Side-blotched lizards (Uta stansburiana) cycle between orange/blue/yellow morphs because each beats one and loses to another. Rare morph wins → frequency rises → loses to next morph in cycle.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-C · MC#7] Side-blotched lizards have three male morphs whose frequencies cycle over years (Orange beats Blue, Blue beats Yellow, Yellow beats Orange). What does this real-world example illustrate?
  A. Negative frequency-dependent selection
  B. Sexual conflict between males and females.
  C. Genetic drift in a small lizard population.
  D. A single ESS dominates and the other strategies disappear.
→ Answer: A

[Final-D · MC#27] MHC genes show extreme polymorphism — some loci have >100 alleles in human populations. The most likely cause is:
  A. Gene conversion homogenizing the locus.
  B. Negative frequency-dependent (balancing) selection from coevolving pathogens
  C. Random mutation alone, with no selection.
  D. Genetic drift in large populations.
→ Answer: B

cards.term: Pit → Cup → Pinhole → Camera — eye in 4 stages
cards.definition:
👁️ NILSSON-PELGER EYE EVOLUTION

📌 The phrase: 4 incremental stages from a flat patch of light-sensitive cells to a fully focused camera eye. Each step is itself functional, addressing the 'irreducible complexity' objection.

◆ PIT — flat patch of photoreceptors gives directional sensitivity. Just better than 'on/off.'
◆ CUP — depression deepens; better directionality, basic shading.
◆ PINHOLE — cup nearly closes; aperture small enough to form a focused image (like nautilus eye today).
◆ CAMERA — lens fills the pinhole, focuses light precisely on retina (vertebrate, octopus eyes).

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Nilsson-Pelger (1994) showed via simulation that going from flat patch to camera eye takes only ~400,000 generations under modest selection — a geological eye-blink. Refutes the claim that complex traits can't evolve gradually.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Eyes evolved 40+ times independently across animals. Vertebrate camera eye, octopus camera eye, insect compound eye, nautilus pinhole — all use different mechanisms but all are useful at every stage.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#28] Critics sometimes object that 'half an eye is useless,' arguing complex traits like eyes can't evolve gradually. What is the strongest evolutionary response?
  A. Eyes evolved in a single dramatic mutation.
  B. The objection is correct, and eye evolution is genuinely mysterious.
  C. Eyes only evolved once in evolutionary history.
  D. Each intermediate stage (light-sensitive patch
→ Answer: D

[Final-C · MC#29] The vertebrate eye and the cephalopod eye are both camera-type eyes with lens, retina, and pupil. They are best described as:
  A. An example of horizontal gene transfer.
  B. Convergent (analogous) structures
  C. Vestigial structures — both eyes are functional,
  D. Homologous structures inherited from a common eyed ancestor.
→ Answer: B

cards.term: Duplicate, Diverge, Discover new function
cards.definition:
🧬 GENE DUPLICATION AS EVOLUTIONARY ENGINE

📌 The phrase: How new genes (and new functions) arise from old ones.

◆ DUPLICATE — gene gets copied (unequal crossover, retrotransposition, whole-genome duplication). Now there are two copies of the same gene.
◆ DIVERGE — one copy keeps the original job (under purifying selection); the other is FREE to mutate without losing original function.
◆ DISCOVER — the redundant copy can acquire new function (neofunctionalization) or split the ancestral function (subfunctionalization).

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Gene duplication is the major source of NEW genes and new functions. Without it, organisms would be stuck with their starting toolkit. Most gene families (globins, opsins, Hox) trace to ancient duplications.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Color vision in primates — the long-wavelength opsin gene duplicated and the copies diverged into red and green opsins, giving trichromatic vision. β-globin family in humans came from ancient duplications of the α-globin ancestor.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-C · MC#19] After a gene duplication event, one copy retains the ancestral function while the other accumulates mutations and eventually evolves a novel role. This is:
  A. Pseudogenization
  B. Gene conversion
  C. Neofunctionalization
  D. Subfunctionalization
→ Answer: C

[Final-A · MC#11] PROTEIN PROMISCUITY refers to:
  A. Proteins frequently interacting with foreign DNA.
  B. Proteins binding multiple partners with equal strength.
  C. Proteins that move freely between cellular compartments.
  D. Proteins having weak side-activities beyond their primary function
→ Answer: D

cards.term: Heterochrony: change the Pace, change the Place
cards.definition:
🧬 HETEROCHRONY — DEVELOPMENTAL TIMING SHIFTS

📌 The phrase: Big morphological evolution often comes from SMALL shifts in WHEN developmental events happen, not from new genes.

◆ PACE — rate of growth/maturation changes. Faster or slower development.
◆ PLACE — timing of stages relative to each other shifts. Sexual maturity arrives earlier or later relative to body growth.

📐 KEY TYPES:
◆ Paedomorphism — adult retains juvenile features (axolotl keeps gills as adult; humans retain juvenile ape skull proportions)
◆ Peramorphism — extends growth into 'super-adult' form (huge antlers of Irish elk)
◆ Neoteny — sexual maturation happens at juvenile body stage

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: A single regulatory mutation can shift timing and produce dramatically different adult morphology — without inventing a new gene. Cheap evolutionary tool.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Mexican axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) reaches sexual maturity while still a 'larva' with gills — paedomorphic. Most salamanders metamorphose to a terrestrial adult; axolotls don't.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#4] Aphids develop into winged or wingless morphs depending on local population density. This is a classic example of:
  A. Inheritance of acquired characteristics.
  B. Independent assortment of alleles at multiple loci.
  C. G×E interaction with no plasticity.
  D. A polyphenic trait
→ Answer: D

[Final-A · MC#2] On a reaction-norm graph (phenotype on y-axis, environment on x-axis), what does a horizontal line for a given genotype indicate?
  A. There is genotype-by-environment interaction.
  B. The trait is environmentally determined and not genetic.
  C. The genotype is plastic — a horizontal line means NO change
  D. The genotype is not plastic
→ Answer: D

cards.term: Hox genes: chromosome order matches body order
cards.definition:
🧬 HOX GENES — DEEP DEVELOPMENTAL HOMOLOGY

📌 The phrase: Hox genes are arranged on the chromosome in the SAME ORDER as the body segments they pattern. Spatial colinearity is maintained from flies to humans.

◆ Hox cluster: Hox1 patterns the head end → Hox13 patterns the tail end
◆ Same order on chromosome = same order along anterior-posterior body axis
◆ The colinearity is conserved across ALL bilaterians — flies, mice, humans share the system

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Hox genes are the master body-plan blueprint. Mutations in them produce homeotic transformations — body parts in wrong places. Reveals that the basic segmentation toolkit is ancient (>500 MY) and shared across animals — DEEP HOMOLOGY.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Antennapedia mutation in Drosophila — Hox gene Antp is misexpressed in the head, causing legs to grow where antennae should be. Bithorax mutation produces 4-winged flies (extra wings instead of halteres).

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-B · MC#24] The same Hox genes pattern the anterior-posterior axis of fruit flies, mice, and humans. What is the strongest evolutionary inference from this fact?
  A. Hox genes evolved independently in flies, mice, and humans through convergence.
  B. Insects and mammals are equally complex — hox conservation is about toolkit, not complexity.
  C. Hox genes were present in the common ancestor of bilaterian animals and have been conserved over hundreds of millions of years.
  D. Hox genes are randomly distributed across animal genomes.
→ Answer: C

[Final-C · MC#29] The vertebrate eye and the cephalopod eye are both camera-type eyes with lens, retina, and pupil. They are best described as:
  A. An example of horizontal gene transfer.
  B. Convergent (analogous) structures
  C. Vestigial structures — both eyes are functional,
  D. Homologous structures inherited from a common eyed ancestor.
→ Answer: B

cards.term: Antagonist Arms Race vs Mutualist Tango
cards.definition:
🦋 TWO MODES OF COEVOLUTION

📌 The phrase: Species evolve in response to each other in two opposite directions.

◆ ANTAGONISTIC ARMS RACE — predator/prey, host/parasite, plant/herbivore. Each species evolves to defeat the other; the other evolves countermeasures. The 'Red Queen' running in place.
◆ MUTUALIST TANGO — both species benefit and depend on each other. Coevolution increases interdependence over time.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Coevolution is one of the strongest drivers of biological diversity. Antagonistic races produce escalating defenses (spines, toxins, immune systems). Mutualistic tangos produce intricate dependencies (figs/wasps, yucca/moth, pollinator/flower coevolution).

🔬 EXAMPLE: Antagonist — Garter snakes evolve resistance to TTX toxin in newts; newts evolve more toxin in response. Mutualist — Each fig species typically pollinated by ONE wasp species; wasps lay eggs only in that fig. Total interdependence.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#12] Rough-skinned newts (Taricha) produce tetrodotoxin (TTX); garter snakes (Thamnophis) eat them. In some regions, snakes are highly TTX-resistant; in others, they have little resistance. What does this geographic variation suggest?
  A. There is a coevolutionary geographic mosaic: 'hotspots' of intense reciprocal selection alternate with 'coldspots' of weak interaction.
  B. Snake populations migrate between regions, equalizing resistance over time.
  C. TTX evolved before snakes evolved resistance, and resistance is still spreading.
  D. Coevolution is not actually occurring — the trait is just genetically variable.
→ Answer: A

[Final-A · MC#28] Which of the following best illustrates coevolution (rather than mere coexistence or convergence)?
  A. Two species of cactus in the same desert evolving similar water-storage tissue.
  B. Two unrelated frogs in different continents evolving the same toxic compound.
  C. Different bird species nesting in the same forest without interacting.
  D. A predator and its prey both evolving faster running speeds in response to one another.
→ Answer: D

cards.term: Bates BLUFFS (one cheats), Müller MUTUAL (both honest)
cards.definition:
🦋 BATESIAN vs MÜLLERIAN MIMICRY

📌 The phrase: Two ways species converge on warning signals, distinguished by whether the mimic is cheating or honest.

◆ BATESIAN — harmless species mimics dangerous one. Tasty viceroy butterflies mimic toxic monarchs. Frequency-dependent: only works if mimic stays RARE relative to model — otherwise predators don't learn the warning.
◆ MÜLLERIAN — multiple genuinely dangerous species converge on a shared warning signal. Heliconius butterflies — many toxic species share the same color pattern. Predators learn faster, BOTH species benefit. Positive frequency-dependence.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Mimicry is among the strongest evidence for selection in action. It also illustrates positive vs negative frequency-dependence in the same broad biological context.

⚠ TRAP: Don't confuse Batesian and Müllerian. Bates = bluff (cheating); Müller = mutual (honest). The B and M letters help.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-B · MC#4] A non-toxic hoverfly evolves yellow-and-black bands resembling a stinging wasp. Predators avoid both. As the hoverfly population grows so that hoverflies become MORE COMMON than wasps, what is most likely to happen?
  A. Predator avoidance becomes stronger because the warning signal is more frequent.
  B. Predator avoidance breaks down because most yellow-and-black insects are actually palatable.
  C. Both species converge further on each other's appearance (Müllerian mimicry).
  D. The hoverfly population stabilizes due to the ESS payoff structure.
→ Answer: B

[Final-A · MC#28] Which of the following best illustrates coevolution (rather than mere coexistence or convergence)?
  A. Two species of cactus in the same desert evolving similar water-storage tissue.
  B. Two unrelated frogs in different continents evolving the same toxic compound.
  C. Different bird species nesting in the same forest without interacting.
  D. A predator and its prey both evolving faster running speeds in response to one another.
→ Answer: D

cards.term: Geographic Mosaic: Hot spots, Cold spots, Trait Mix
cards.definition:
🗺️ THOMPSON'S GEOGRAPHIC MOSAIC THEORY OF COEVOLUTION

📌 The phrase: Coevolution doesn't happen uniformly across a species' range. It's PATCHY.

◆ HOT SPOTS — populations where the two species strongly select on each other. Reciprocal coevolution intense.
◆ COLD SPOTS — populations where the interaction is weak or absent. No coevolution happening.
◆ TRAIT MIX — gene flow shuffles traits between hot and cold spots, creating a constantly remixed mosaic across the range.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Explains why coevolved traits look messy and asymmetric across a species' range — the local 'fit' between two species varies enormously. Also explains why some populations stay coevolutionarily 'naive' while others are tightly engaged.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Crossbill birds vs lodgepole pine cones in Rocky Mountains. Where both species are present (hot spot), cones evolve thicker scales and bills evolve to crack them. Where squirrels are also present (cold spot for crossbills), cones evolve different defenses against squirrels instead.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#12] Rough-skinned newts (Taricha) produce tetrodotoxin (TTX); garter snakes (Thamnophis) eat them. In some regions, snakes are highly TTX-resistant; in others, they have little resistance. What does this geographic variation suggest?
  A. There is a coevolutionary geographic mosaic: 'hotspots' of intense reciprocal selection alternate with 'coldspots' of weak interaction.
  B. Snake populations migrate between regions, equalizing resistance over time.
  C. TTX evolved before snakes evolved resistance, and resistance is still spreading.
  D. Coevolution is not actually occurring — the trait is just genetically variable.
→ Answer: A

[Final-A · MC#28] Which of the following best illustrates coevolution (rather than mere coexistence or convergence)?
  A. Two species of cactus in the same desert evolving similar water-storage tissue.
  B. Two unrelated frogs in different continents evolving the same toxic compound.
  C. Different bird species nesting in the same forest without interacting.
  D. A predator and its prey both evolving faster running speeds in response to one another.
→ Answer: D

cards.term: Sex pays for itself with the Red Queen and Muller's Ratchet
cards.definition:
⚥ WHY SEX EVOLVED DESPITE THE 2-FOLD COST

📌 The phrase: Sexual reproduction has a 2-fold cost (you pass on only half your genes, plus you need to find a mate, plus STDs). Yet most eukaryotes do it. These two hypotheses explain why.

◆ RED QUEEN — Parasites and hosts coevolve. Parasites adapt to common host genotypes; sex creates new genotypes via recombination, keeping hosts ahead. From Lewis Carroll: 'It takes all the running you can do, to keep in the same place.'
◆ MULLER'S RATCHET — In asexual lineages, deleterious mutations only accumulate (no way to combine pure-germline genomes). Sex + recombination can REASSEMBLE clean genomes from two parents. Asexual species grind down via the ratchet.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Sex is ubiquitous despite the cost — these two mechanisms explain the maintenance of sex over evolutionary time.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Bdelloid rotifers (asexual for 80+ MY) are the famous exception, but they survive partly via massive horizontal gene transfer and unusual genome repair — they cheat the ratchet by other means.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#19] The Red Queen hypothesis proposes that sexual reproduction is favored because:
  A. Predators preferentially attack asexual species.
  B. Sex makes reproduction faster than asexual processes.
  C. Sexual reproduction reduces parental investment in each offspring.
  D. Hosts must constantly evolve to keep up with rapidly evolving parasites
→ Answer: D

[Final-D · MC#11] Muller's ratchet describes:
  A. Loss of beneficial alleles by drift in small sexual populations.
  B. The clicking sound of bacterial flagella.
  C. A directional ratchet of beneficial mutations in sexual populations.
  D. Irreversible accumulation of deleterious mutations in asexual populations
→ Answer: D

cards.term: Anisogamy: Eggs Expensive, Sperm Cheap
cards.definition:
⚥ THE FOUNDATION OF MALE/FEMALE

📌 The phrase: One asymmetry — different gamete sizes — seeds nearly all of sexual selection theory.

◆ EGGS EXPENSIVE — large, energetically costly, few in number. Definition of 'female' = the sex with the bigger gamete.
◆ SPERM CHEAP — small, energetically minor, abundant. Definition of 'male' = the sex with the smaller gamete.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Anisogamy is THE root of all sex-related asymmetries:
→ Females become the LIMITING resource (eggs are scarce)
→ Males compete for access to females
→ Females become the CHOOSY sex
→ Sexual dimorphism, courtship, ornaments — all flow from this single asymmetry

🔬 EXAMPLE: When sex roles reverse (e.g., seahorses where males brood), the choosy/ornamented sex flips with them — confirming the link to gamete investment, not genitalia per se.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-C · MC#16] Biologically, the FEMALE in a sexually reproducing species is defined as:
  A. The sex that bears live offspring.
  B. The sex that has two X chromosomes.
  C. The sex that displays mate choice.
  D. The sex that produces the larger, costlier gamete.
→ Answer: D

[Final-A · MC#30] Male elk grow large antlers used in physical combat with rival males during the breeding season. This is primarily an example of:
  A. Sexual conflict — sexual conflict is between
  B. Intrasexual selection (same-sex competition).
  C. Intersexual selection (mate choice).
  D. Sexual cooperation — combat is competitive, not
→ Answer: B

cards.term: Bateman: Females limited by Eggs, Males limited by Mates
cards.definition:
⚥ BATEMAN'S PRINCIPLE

📌 The phrase: Female and male reproductive success are limited by different things. This asymmetry generates almost all sexual dimorphism.

◆ FEMALES LIMITED BY EGGS — reproductive output saturates fast. One mate is usually enough. Quality of mate matters more than quantity → CHOOSY.
◆ MALES LIMITED BY MATES — reproductive output keeps climbing with more mates. Quantity matters → COMPETITIVE.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: This is the single principle from which most predictions about sexual dimorphism, mate choice, and competition follow. Originally established by Angus Bateman (1948) using Drosophila experiments showing variance in male reproductive success ≫ variance in female RS.

📐 BATEMAN GRADIENT: slope of reproductive success on number of mates. Steep for males (each extra mate adds offspring); flat for females (offspring number is set by eggs).

⚠ TRAP: Sex roles can REVERSE when male parental investment exceeds female (seahorses, some shorebirds, jacanas). Then females compete and males choose.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-B · MC#10] Species in which females mate with multiple males within a single breeding cycle tend to evolve relatively LARGE TESTES compared to species with strictly monogamous mating. The most likely explanation is:
  A. Sperm competition — males who produce more sperm have higher chances of fertilizing ova when ejaculate from rival males is also present.
  B. Larger testes are required for hormone signaling.
  C. Larger testes evolved randomly via drift — the pattern is too strong and consistent across
  D. Larger testes in polyandrous species support larger overall body size.
→ Answer: A

[Final-C · MC#22] Female peahens prefer males with larger, more iridescent tails. Male peacock tails reduce survival (visible to predators, costly to grow). The persistence of the tail despite its survival cost is best explained by:
  A. Intersexual selection (mate choice) outweighing the survival cost.
  B. Group selection for showy populations — group selection isn't needed
  C. Intrasexual selection — males physically fight with their tails.
  D. Sexual conflict — females can't tell males with tails apart from males without.
→ Answer: A

cards.term: FZH Choice: Fisher Runs, Zahavi Handicaps, Hamilton-Zuk Parasites
cards.definition:
⚥ THREE HYPOTHESES FOR FEMALE MATE CHOICE

📌 The phrase: Three (non-exclusive) reasons females might prefer ornamented males.

◆ FISHER'S RUNAWAY — preference genes and trait genes get linked through assortative mating. Daughters of choosy mothers + showy fathers inherit BOTH preference and trait. Positive feedback drives the trait to extreme — 'sexy sons.' No need for the trait to indicate quality.
◆ ZAHAVI'S HANDICAP — the ornament is COSTLY to produce/maintain. Only genuinely high-quality males can afford it without dying. The cost makes the signal HONEST. Wasteful = trustworthy.
◆ HAMILTON-ZUK — bright color, energetic display, etc., signal RESISTANCE TO PARASITES. Only parasite-free males can mount the display. Females choosing showy males get good (parasite-resistant) genes for their offspring.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: These aren't competing — they can all act simultaneously. Different traits in different species are best explained by different mechanisms.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Peacock tail = often interpreted as Zahavi handicap (huge cost). House finch red plumage = Hamilton-Zuk (carotenoids signal parasite/diet quality). Long tail of widowbirds = Fisher runaway evidence (Andersson's classic 1982 experiment).

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-B · MC#22] Fisherian runaway sexual selection refers to:
  A. Mutation pressure generating new ornament traits.
  B. A positive-feedback process where female preference for a male trait and the trait itself co-amplify over generations
  C. Predators learning to avoid mating displays of unpalatable species.
  D. Loss of all sexual ornaments due to high predation.
→ Answer: B

[Final-C · MC#22] Female peahens prefer males with larger, more iridescent tails. Male peacock tails reduce survival (visible to predators, costly to grow). The persistence of the tail despite its survival cost is best explained by:
  A. Intersexual selection (mate choice) outweighing the survival cost.
  B. Group selection for showy populations — group selection isn't needed
  C. Intrasexual selection — males physically fight with their tails.
  D. Sexual conflict — females can't tell males with tails apart from males without.
→ Answer: A

cards.term: High Extrinsic Mortality → Live Fast, Die Young; Low → Live Slow, Die Old
cards.definition:
⏳ LIFE-HISTORY CORE PRINCIPLE

📌 The phrase: How dangerous your environment is shapes your life-history strategy. If something else is going to kill you, evolve to reproduce fast.

◆ HIGH EXTRINSIC MORTALITY → predators or environment kill you regardless of how careful you are. Selection favors EARLY, FAST reproduction. Don't invest in long life — you won't get to enjoy it.
◆ LOW EXTRINSIC MORTALITY → if you stay healthy, you'll live a long time. Selection favors slow growth, late maturation, repeated reproduction. INVEST IN MAINTENANCE.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: This single principle explains why mice live 1-2 years and elephants live 60. Mice have high extrinsic mortality (predators); elephants don't (apex herbivore). Evolution has tuned each species' rate of aging to match its risk profile.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Greenland sharks (~400 yr lifespan), bowhead whales, naked mole rats — all have low extrinsic mortality, slow aging. Pacific salmon — high adult mortality post-spawning, evolved to die after one breeding event (semelparity).

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#1] Two populations of guppies live in adjacent pools. Pool A has heavy predator presence; Pool B has no predators. What life-history difference would you predict?
  A. Pool A guppies have longer lifespans because they're tougher.
  B. Pool A guppies mature LATER and produce FEWER offspring.
  C. Pool A guppies mature EARLIER and produce MORE offspring.
  D. No difference — life history is genetically fixed.
→ Answer: C

[Final-A · MC#12] Salmon reproduce once in a single massive spawning event and die shortly afterward (semelparity). What life-history logic best explains this strategy?
  A. Multiple breeding events are forbidden by Pacific Ocean conditions.
  B. Salmon are too dumb to live longer than one breeding season.
  C. Adult salmon survival is so low after migration that maximum effort in a single reproductive bout outperforms hedging across multiple bouts.
  D. Salmon are unable to reproduce more than once due to a genetic defect.
→ Answer: C

cards.term: r vs K: r = many small (rats), K = few big (elephants)
cards.definition:
⏳ r-SELECTION vs K-SELECTION

📌 The phrase: Two ends of a life-history strategy continuum, named after the parameters of logistic growth.

◆ r-SELECTED — high intrinsic growth rate (r). Many offspring, little parental care, small body, fast maturation, short life. Thrives in unpredictable, disturbed environments. Examples: rodents, weeds, insects, opportunistic species.
◆ K-SELECTED — adapted to carrying capacity (K). Few offspring, heavy parental investment, large body, slow maturation, long life. Wins in stable, competitive environments. Examples: elephants, oaks, whales, primates.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Predicts how species respond to disturbance. r-strategists colonize quickly after disasters; K-strategists dominate stable habitats but recover slowly from population crashes.

⚠ TRAP: r/K is a continuum, not a dichotomy. Most modern texts prefer 'fast vs slow life history' to avoid the assumption that species sit cleanly at one end.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-B · MC#27] An r-selected species would typically display which combination of traits?
  A. One offspring per lifetime, no maturity stage, immortality.
  B. Few offspring, late maturity, parental care, long lifespan.
  C. Many offspring, early maturity, little parental care, short lifespan.
  D. Sterile workers and a single reproductive queen.
→ Answer: C

[Final-D · MC#1] Two populations of guppies live in adjacent pools. Pool A has heavy predator presence; Pool B has no predators. What life-history difference would you predict?
  A. Pool A guppies have longer lifespans because they're tougher.
  B. Pool A guppies mature LATER and produce FEWER offspring.
  C. Pool A guppies mature EARLIER and produce MORE offspring.
  D. No difference — life history is genetically fixed.
→ Answer: C

cards.term: Why we age: Medawar Hides, Williams Trades, Kirkwood Disposes
cards.definition:
⏳ THREE EVOLUTIONARY THEORIES OF SENESCENCE

📌 The phrase: Why does aging exist if natural selection should oppose it? Three (compatible) answers.

◆ MEDAWAR HIDES — Mutation Accumulation theory. Late-acting deleterious mutations are mostly INVISIBLE to selection because most carriers have already reproduced. Bad late genes accumulate in the genome.
◆ WILLIAMS TRADES — Antagonistic Pleiotropy. Some genes are GOOD early in life (high fertility, fast growth) but BAD late in life (cancer, heart disease). Selection favors them because the early benefit comes when selection is strong; the late cost is paid when selection is weak.
◆ KIRKWOOD DISPOSES — Disposable Soma theory. Energy is finite. Resources spent on reproduction can't be spent on maintenance. Evolution invests in the GERMLINE; the body (soma) is expendable.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Aging isn't a 'failure' of evolution — it's a predictable outcome of selection's weakening with age. Explains why long-lived organisms (whales, tortoises) tend to be those with low extrinsic mortality (selection stays strong longer).

🔬 EXAMPLE: BRCA1/2 alleles can be antagonistic-pleiotropy candidates — possibly favored historically for early-life effects despite raising late-life cancer risk. Naked mole rats appear to dodge typical aging via specialized cellular maintenance — costly investment that pays off because they have very low extrinsic mortality.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-C · MC#20] Medawar's mutation accumulation theory of aging proposes that:
  A. Each species has a fixed number of cell divisions.
  B. Mutations are more common in older individuals.
  C. Late-acting deleterious mutations escape selection and accumulate in the gene pool
  D. Aging is caused by accumulation of toxins.
→ Answer: C

[Final-A · MC#5] Most cancers occur in older individuals. From an evolutionary perspective, why has selection failed to eliminate cancer susceptibility?
  A. Cancer is contagious in some species.
  B. Cancer was unknown in ancestral populations.
  C. All organisms have an upper age limit.
  D. Selection's strength declines with age
→ Answer: D

cards.term: rB > C — relatedness × benefit beats cost
cards.definition:
🤝 HAMILTON'S RULE — INCLUSIVE FITNESS

📌 The phrase: An altruistic act is favored by selection when (relatedness × benefit to recipient) exceeds (cost to actor).

◆ r — coefficient of relatedness. Probability that a given allele in actor is shared by descent in recipient. Twins r=1, sibs ½, half-sibs ¼, cousins ⅛. Honeybee sisters (haplodiploid) r=¾.
◆ B — fitness benefit to the recipient (in offspring units)
◆ C — fitness cost to the actor (in offspring units)

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Hamilton's Rule (1964) resolves the apparent paradox of altruism. A 'selfish gene' can favor altruistic BEHAVIOR if the helped individuals carry copies of itself. Explains:
→ Alarm calls (warn relatives, attract predator to self)
→ Sterile castes in social insects (workers raise siblings)
→ Helpers-at-the-nest in birds (delay own breeding to help parents)
→ Eusociality

🧮 INCLUSIVE FITNESS = direct fitness (own offspring) + indirect fitness (extra relatives produced via helping).

🔬 EXAMPLE: Belding's ground squirrel alarm calls — females call more than males because females are more related to neighbors (philopatric); males disperse so neighbors are unrelated.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-C · MC#3] Hamilton's rule for the evolution of altruism is:
  A. C > rB
  B. B > C
  C. B = C
  D. rB > C
→ Answer: D

[Final-A · MC#25] Worker honey bees forgo reproduction and help raise their queen's offspring. From an inclusive-fitness perspective, this makes sense because:
  A. Workers are sterile and incapable of reproduction.
  B. Workers gain inclusive fitness by helping raise sisters (in haplodiploid systems
  C. Group selection at the colony level overrides individual fitness.
  D. Workers are forced into helping by the queen and have no choice.
→ Answer: B

cards.term: Side-blotched lizards: Orange beats Blue, Blue beats Yellow, Yellow beats Orange
cards.definition:
🦎 ROCK-PAPER-SCISSORS IN NATURE

📌 The phrase: Three throat-color morphs of male side-blotched lizards (Uta stansburiana) cycle in frequency because each beats one and loses to another. NEGATIVE frequency-dependent selection.

◆ ORANGE — aggressive bully. Large territory, multiple females. BEATS Blue by overpowering smaller territory holders.
◆ BLUE — pair-bonder/mate-guarder. Defends one female. BEATS Yellow because mate-guarding stops sneaking; partners cooperate.
◆ YELLOW — sneaker. Mimics female coloration to slip past dominant males. BEATS Orange because Orange can't watch all his females at once.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Empirical demonstration of:
→ Negative frequency-dependent selection
→ Multiple equilibria/cycling, not fixation
→ How ESS theory plays out in nature with non-transitive payoffs

Whichever morph becomes rare gains a fitness advantage. The frequencies cycle on roughly 4-6 year periods.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Sinervo & Lively (1996, Nature) tracked frequencies in California populations and showed clean cycling consistent with the RPS prediction.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-C · MC#7] Side-blotched lizards have three male morphs whose frequencies cycle over years (Orange beats Blue, Blue beats Yellow, Yellow beats Orange). What does this real-world example illustrate?
  A. Negative frequency-dependent selection
  B. Sexual conflict between males and females.
  C. Genetic drift in a small lizard population.
  D. A single ESS dominates and the other strategies disappear.
→ Answer: A

[Final-D · MC#27] MHC genes show extreme polymorphism — some loci have >100 alleles in human populations. The most likely cause is:
  A. Gene conversion homogenizing the locus.
  B. Negative frequency-dependent (balancing) selection from coevolving pathogens
  C. Random mutation alone, with no selection.
  D. Genetic drift in large populations.
→ Answer: B

cards.term: ESS = Strategy that, once common, can't be invaded
cards.definition:
🤝 EVOLUTIONARILY STABLE STRATEGY

📌 The phrase: An ESS is a strategy such that, if all members of a population adopt it, no rare alternative strategy can invade and spread. The game-theoretic definition of evolutionary stability.

◆ A strategy is ESS if it is the best response to itself when common.
◆ Mutants playing different strategies have lower fitness than ESS-players.

📐 HAWK-DOVE GAME (Maynard Smith & Price 1973):
→ Hawk: always escalates fight
→ Dove: always backs down
→ Hawk vs Hawk = costly injury (-C/2)
→ Dove vs Dove = share resource (+V/2)
→ Hawk vs Dove = Hawk wins (+V), Dove gets 0

If C > V: pure Hawk is NOT ESS (Hawks injure each other); equilibrium is a mixed strategy or genetic polymorphism.
If C < V: Hawk IS ESS (always pays to fight).

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: ESS is the central concept in evolutionary game theory. It tells you what frequency-dependent equilibrium will look like. Used to model conflicts, cooperation, signaling, sex ratios, foraging — anywhere fitness depends on what others are doing.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Side-blotched lizards have NO single ESS — they cycle through morphs. Most species' male/female ratios are at the ESS predicted by Fisher's sex-ratio argument (1:1).

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-C · MC#4] An Evolutionarily Stable Strategy (ESS) is best defined as:
  A. A strategy that produces the most offspring on average.
  B. A strategy that, when adopted by most members of a population, cannot be invaded by any rare alternative strategy.
  C. The strategy that maximizes population mean fitness.
  D. A strategy that always wins in head-to-head competition.
→ Answer: B

[Final-B · MC#20] In a Hawk-Dove game, why doesn't a population evolve to be entirely Hawks (always-aggressive)?
  A. When Hawks are common, Hawk-Hawk fights inflict heavy costs
  B. All-Hawk populations are never possible due to genetic constraints.
  C. Doves are intrinsically more fit in all environments.
  D. Group selection penalizes aggressive populations.
→ Answer: A

cards.term: Cooperation among non-kin: Reciprocity, Reputation, Byproduct
cards.definition:
🤝 NON-KIN COOPERATION (NO HAMILTON'S RULE NEEDED)

📌 The phrase: Three mechanisms by which cooperation can evolve between unrelated individuals.

◆ RECIPROCITY (DIRECT) — Trivers's reciprocal altruism. 'You scratch my back, I'll scratch yours.' Tit-for-tat strategy. Requires repeated interactions, recognition of partners. Vampire bats sharing blood meals.
◆ REPUTATION (INDIRECT RECIPROCITY) — Helping someone in front of others builds your reputation; observers later help you. Doesn't require reciprocity from the helped individual — third parties pay you forward. Strong in humans.
◆ BYPRODUCT MUTUALISM — both individuals benefit just from each other's presence/activity. No cost to either; no cheating possible. Common in cleaner fish, mixed-species foraging flocks.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Hamilton's rule explains kin cooperation, but most human cooperation is among non-kin. These three mechanisms (plus group selection in some frameworks) cover the gap.

⚠ TRAP: Pure reciprocity can be unstable — defectors profit. That's why repeat interactions, reputation systems, and punishment mechanisms commonly co-evolve with reciprocity.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-C · MC#17] Vampire bats regurgitate blood to feed roost-mates who failed to feed that night. Recipients later return the favor when they have surplus and the original donor goes hungry. This best illustrates:
  A. Naïve group selection.
  B. Inclusive fitness through close kinship only.
  C. DIRECT reciprocity
  D. Sexual conflict.
→ Answer: C

[Final-A · MC#25] Worker honey bees forgo reproduction and help raise their queen's offspring. From an inclusive-fitness perspective, this makes sense because:
  A. Workers are sterile and incapable of reproduction.
  B. Workers gain inclusive fitness by helping raise sisters (in haplodiploid systems
  C. Group selection at the colony level overrides individual fitness.
  D. Workers are forced into helping by the queen and have no choice.
→ Answer: B

cards.term: 4 EONS: Hadean Hell, Archean Ancient, Proterozoic Pre-life-explosion, Phanerozoic Visible-life
cards.definition:
🌌 THE 4 EONS OF EARTH HISTORY

📌 The phrase: Earth's 4.6 BY history broken into 4 great eons, each with its own character.

◆ HADEAN (4.6 - 4.0 BYA) — 'Hellish.' Molten Earth, no rocks survive. Late Heavy Bombardment.
◆ ARCHEAN (4.0 - 2.5 BYA) — 'Ancient.' First prokaryotes. No oxygen in atmosphere. Stromatolites form.
◆ PROTEROZOIC (2.5 BYA - 540 MYA) — 'Pre-Cambrian-explosion.' Great Oxidation Event ~2.4 BYA. First eukaryotes. Snowball Earth events. First multicellular animals (Ediacaran).
◆ PHANEROZOIC (540 MYA - now) — 'Visible-life.' Hard-shelled animals leave abundant fossils. The 'animal-rich' eon. Subdivided into Paleozoic, Mesozoic, Cenozoic.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Sets the SCAFFOLD for all evolutionary history. ~88% of Earth's history is pre-Phanerozoic — most of life's history predates the fossil record we see in textbooks.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Great Oxidation Event (~2.4 BYA, in Proterozoic) — cyanobacteria producing O₂ poisoned anaerobes and set the stage for aerobic eukaryotes. The biggest atmospheric change in Earth's history.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#10] Earth is approximately how old, based on radiometric dating?
  A. 100 million years
  B. 4.568 billion years
  C. 13.8 billion years
  D. 4.568 million years
→ Answer: B

[Final-B · MC#25] The Cambrian explosion (~541 MYA) refers to:
  A. The first appearance of plants.
  B. A nuclear-scale extinction event in the Cambrian.
  C. A volcanic eruption that ended the Cambrian.
  D. The rapid (~20 MYR) appearance of most modern animal phyla in the fossil record.
→ Answer: D

cards.term: PHANEROZOIC PERIODS — year + event for each
cards.definition:
🌌 THE 10 PHANEROZOIC PERIODS WITH KEY EVENTS

📌 The phrase: From the Cambrian explosion to today, with what defined each period.

◆ 540 MYA — CAMBRIAN — 'Cambrian Crashes-in.' Body plans EXPLODE. All major animal phyla appear in ~30 MY.
◆ 485 — ORDOVICIAN — 'Ocean fish Organize.' First jawless fish. Ends in glaciation extinction.
◆ 444 — SILURIAN — 'Silurian Sets-stage on land.' Plants and arthropods invade land.
◆ 419 — DEVONIAN — 'AGE of FISH.' Tiktaalik (375 MYA) — fish-tetrapod transitional. Tetrapods crawl onto land.
◆ 359 — CARBONIFEROUS — 'Coal forests, Colossal insects.' High O₂ enables giant dragonflies (Meganeura, 70 cm wingspan). Coal beds form from buried plant matter.
◆ 299 — PERMIAN — 'Pangaea + GREAT DYING.' Supercontinent assembles. Ends 252 MYA with the largest mass extinction in Earth's history (96% marine species lost).
◆ 252 — TRIASSIC — 'Tiny mammals, Tyrant lizards rise.' First dinosaurs. First true mammals (shrew-sized).
◆ 201 — JURASSIC — 'Just dinosaurs.' Dinosaur dominance. Birds emerge from theropods (Archaeopteryx ~150 MYA).
◆ 145 — CRETACEOUS — 'T. rex, ENDS at K-Pg 66.' Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary. Chicxulub asteroid impact in Yucatán wipes out non-avian dinosaurs.
◆ 66 — CENOZOIC — 'Mammals & primates radiate.' Cenozoic Era ('Age of Mammals'). Hominins emerge in last 7 MY.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Every fossil and every evolutionary milestone is anchored to one of these periods. Knowing the year + the headline event for each is the bare minimum for evolutionary literacy.

⚠ TRAP: 'Tertiary' is the older name; 'Cenozoic' (or Paleogene + Neogene + Quaternary) is current usage. K-Pg replaced K-T.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#22] The Devonian period (~416–359 MYA) is most associated with which biological event?
  A. The first dinosaurs.
  B. Diversification of fishes and the origin of land vertebrates (early tetrapods).
  C. The Cambrian explosion.
  D. The first land plants.
→ Answer: B

[Final-D · MC#30] The Silurian period (~444–416 MYA) is best known for:
  A. The K-T extinction event.
  B. The origin of mammals.
  C. The first land animals (e.g.
  D. The first photosynthetic life.
→ Answer: C

cards.term: Endosymbiosis: Mitochondria from α-proteobacteria, Chloroplasts from cyanobacteria
cards.definition:
🌌 ENDOSYMBIOTIC THEORY (LYNN MARGULIS)

📌 The phrase: Eukaryotic organelles weren't built — they were ENGULFED. Mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living bacteria.

◆ MITOCHONDRIA — descended from an α-proteobacterium engulfed by an archaeal host ~1.5-2 BYA. Provided aerobic respiration.
◆ CHLOROPLASTS — descended from a cyanobacterium engulfed by an early eukaryote ~1 BYA. Provided photosynthesis.

📐 EVIDENCE FOR ENDOSYMBIOSIS:
→ Double membranes (inner = bacterial, outer = host-derived)
→ Own circular DNA, like bacteria
→ 70S ribosomes (bacterial type), not 80S
→ Reproduce by binary fission, independently of cell
→ Size matches free-living bacteria
→ Antibiotics that target bacteria also affect mitochondria/chloroplasts

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Endosymbiosis is THE founding event of complex life. Without mitochondria, no eukaryotes; without eukaryotes, no animals or plants. Lynn Margulis's theory was rejected for decades before molecular evidence vindicated it.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Plastid genomes still resemble cyanobacterial genomes; mitochondrial genomes still resemble Rickettsia-like α-proteobacterial genomes. mtDNA's bacterial origin is also why it's used in maternal lineage tracing.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#10] Earth is approximately how old, based on radiometric dating?
  A. 100 million years
  B. 4.568 billion years
  C. 13.8 billion years
  D. 4.568 million years
→ Answer: B

[Final-B · MC#25] The Cambrian explosion (~541 MYA) refers to:
  A. The first appearance of plants.
  B. A nuclear-scale extinction event in the Cambrian.
  C. A volcanic eruption that ended the Cambrian.
  D. The rapid (~20 MYR) appearance of most modern animal phyla in the fossil record.
→ Answer: D

cards.term: Woese's 3 Domains: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya
cards.definition:
🌌 THE THREE-DOMAIN SYSTEM (CARL WOESE, 1977)

📌 The phrase: The deepest division of life is NOT prokaryote vs eukaryote. It's BACTERIA vs ARCHAEA vs EUKARYA.

◆ BACTERIA — true bacteria. Peptidoglycan cell walls. Ester-linked lipid membranes.
◆ ARCHAEA — superficially look like bacteria but molecularly very different. Ether-linked branched lipids. Often extremophiles (hyperthermophiles, halophiles, methanogens). MORE related to eukaryotes than to bacteria!
◆ EUKARYA — cells with nuclei. Plants, animals, fungi, protists. Branched off from within Archaea (specifically the Asgard clade).

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Reorganized the tree of life. The old 5-kingdom system (Plantae/Animalia/Fungi/Protista/Monera) is wrong at the deepest level — it lumped Archaea and Bacteria as 'Monera' even though they diverged before Bacteria-Eukarya did.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Woese used 16S/18S ribosomal RNA sequences (highly conserved, slow-evolving) to compare deep relationships. The molecular tree showed Archaea were a separate group, fundamentally different from Bacteria despite morphological similarity.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#10] Earth is approximately how old, based on radiometric dating?
  A. 100 million years
  B. 4.568 billion years
  C. 13.8 billion years
  D. 4.568 million years
→ Answer: B

[Final-B · MC#25] The Cambrian explosion (~541 MYA) refers to:
  A. The first appearance of plants.
  B. A nuclear-scale extinction event in the Cambrian.
  C. A volcanic eruption that ended the Cambrian.
  D. The rapid (~20 MYR) appearance of most modern animal phyla in the fossil record.
→ Answer: D

cards.term: O-D-P-Tr-K — Old Dinosaurs Probably Took K-Pg
cards.definition:
🦖 THE BIG 5 MASS EXTINCTIONS

📌 The phrase: Five mass extinctions in the Phanerozoic, oldest to youngest. PERMIAN was the worst. K-Pg the most famous.

◆ ORDOVICIAN (~445 MYA) — Glaciation, sea-level drop. Marine animals decimated.
◆ DEVONIAN (~375 MYA) — Multiple pulses. Anoxia in oceans. Lost reef systems.
◆ PERMIAN (~252 MYA) — 'GREAT DYING.' Siberian Traps volcanism, ocean anoxia, climate chaos. ~96% marine species, ~70% terrestrial vertebrates lost. THE BIGGEST. Took 10 MY for biodiversity to recover.
◆ TRIASSIC-JURASSIC (~201 MYA) — Volcanism (Central Atlantic Magmatic Province). Cleared the way for dinosaur dominance.
◆ K-Pg (~66 MYA) — Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary. Chicxulub asteroid impact in Yucatán + Deccan Traps volcanism. Ended non-avian dinosaurs and ammonites; opened niches for mammal radiation.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Each extinction RESET the ecosystem. Survivors radiated into vacated niches. Mass extinctions are the punctuated 'reset buttons' between long periods of relative stasis. We're living through the 6th — anthropogenic — right now.

⚠ TRAP: K-Pg gets the headlines because of dinosaurs, but the PERMIAN was much worse — it was the closest life on Earth ever came to total ecological collapse.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-B · MC#18] Which of the following is NOT one of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions?
  A. End-Cretaceous / K-Pg (~66 MYA).
  B. End-Pleistocene (~11 KYA megafauna extinction).
  C. End-Permian (~252 MYA).
  D. End-Triassic (~201 MYA).
→ Answer: B

[Final-D · MC#20] The largest mass extinction in Earth's history occurred at the:
  A. Cambrian explosion, ~541 MYA — the Cambrian explosion is
  B. End of the Cretaceous, killing all dinosaurs.
  C. K-T (K-Pg) boundary, ~66 MYA, due to asteroid impact.
  D. End of the Permian, ~252 MYA, eliminating ~95% of marine species.
→ Answer: D

cards.term: 3 Character Types: Synapomorphy is Gold, Symplesiomorphy is Worthless, Homoplasy is False
cards.definition:
🌳 PHYLOGENETIC CHARACTERS — WHICH ONES CARRY INFORMATION

📌 The phrase: Three kinds of trait similarity, only ONE is useful for building trees.

◆ SYNAPOMORPHY — SHARED DERIVED character. Defines a clade. The grouping signal cladistics is built on. Example: feathers (in modern context — uniquely shared by all birds and no others).
◆ SYMPLESIOMORPHY — SHARED ANCIENT character. Worthless for clade-finding because it's shared more broadly than the clade you're trying to find. Example: 'has a vertebral column' — true of all vertebrates, doesn't help group fish vs mammals.
◆ HOMOPLASY — convergent or parallel similarity. LOOKS like homology but isn't — independently evolved. Misleading signal. Example: bird wings + bat wings + insect wings — all wings, but not from a winged ancestor.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: This three-way distinction is the CORE of cladistic methodology. Modern phylogenetics uses statistical methods that try to maximize synapomorphy signal and minimize homoplasy.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Mammals + birds both have a 4-chambered heart (homoplasy — evolved independently). Mammals + reptiles share amniotic egg (synapomorphy that defines Amniota). 'Vertebrates that fly' (mammals + birds) is polyphyletic because flight is homoplastic.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#23] You're trying to define a clade containing only mammals. 'Has a vertebral column' is a shared trait among all your candidate species. What is this character at the level of mammals?
  A. Diagnostic of all mammals but not informative for non-mammalian relatives.
  B. A synapomorphy uniting mammals — it's not novel to mammals
  C. A symplesiomorphy — present in the deeper ancestor of all vertebrates
  D. A homoplasy — independently evolved in different mammalian lineages.
→ Answer: C

[Final-C · MC#29] The vertebrate eye and the cephalopod eye are both camera-type eyes with lens, retina, and pupil. They are best described as:
  A. An example of horizontal gene transfer.
  B. Convergent (analogous) structures
  C. Vestigial structures — both eyes are functional,
  D. Homologous structures inherited from a common eyed ancestor.
→ Answer: B

cards.term: 3 Clade Types: Mom + ALL kids = good (Monophyletic ✓)
cards.definition:
🌳 MONO / PARA / POLY — VALIDITY OF GROUPS

📌 The phrase: Three ways to draw a circle on a tree. Only Monophyletic is valid in modern systematics.

◆ MONOPHYLETIC ✓ — ancestor + ALL descendants. A 'clade' or 'natural group.' Defined by synapomorphies. Examples: Mammals, Birds, Insects, all valid clades.
◆ PARAPHYLETIC ✗ — ancestor + SOME descendants (one or more groups EXCLUDED). The classic 'Reptilia' (when birds are excluded) is paraphyletic because birds descended from within reptiles. 'Fish' (excluding tetrapods) is paraphyletic. Modern taxonomy avoids these.
◆ POLYPHYLETIC ✗ — group whose members do NOT share a recent common ancestor. The trait used to group them is HOMOPLASTIC. Example: 'Warm-blooded animals' = mammals + birds, but warm-bloodedness evolved independently. Worst kind of grouping.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: A core test on every phylogeny exam. Decides which named groups are scientifically valid (monophyletic) vs traditional but technically wrong (paraphyletic) vs just incoherent (polyphyletic).

🔬 EXAMPLE: 'Dinosauria' INCLUDING birds = monophyletic ✓. 'Dinosauria' excluding birds = paraphyletic ✗. 'Animals that fly' = polyphyletic ✗.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-B · MC#21] The traditional group 'Reptilia' (turtles, lizards, snakes, crocodiles) excludes birds. Birds, however, are descended from theropod dinosaurs, nested within Reptilia by descent. What kind of group is traditional 'Reptilia'?
  A. Diphyletic — has exactly two ancestral origins.
  B. Polyphyletic — members lack an immediate common ancestor.
  C. Paraphyletic — includes a common ancestor and SOME but not all of its descendants.
  D. Monophyletic — it's a clade — a clade includes ALL descendants
→ Answer: C

[Final-A · MC#24] On a phylogenetic tree, two taxa are 'more closely related' to each other than to a third when:
  A. Their lineages have evolved at similar rates.
  B. Their branches end closer together horizontally on the page.
  C. They share a more recent common ancestor (a more shallow node) than either does with the third.
  D. They share more morphological similarities overall.
→ Answer: C

cards.term: BMP — Biological, Morphological, Phylogenetic
cards.definition:
🐦 THE 3 MAIN SPECIES CONCEPTS

📌 The phrase: Three different definitions of 'species,' each with strengths and weaknesses. No single definition works in all cases.

◆ BIOLOGICAL (Mayr 1942) — species = group whose members can interbreed and produce fertile offspring, reproductively isolated from other such groups. Cleanest concept for sexually reproducing animals. CAN'T apply to fossils (no breeding observable) or asexuals.
◆ MORPHOLOGICAL — species defined by appearance/morphology. Works on fossils. Misses cryptic species (look identical, don't interbreed) and inflates polymorphic species into multiple 'species.'
◆ PHYLOGENETIC — smallest monophyletic group identifiable from a phylogeny. Works on any organisms. Tends to identify MORE species than BSC (any consistent diagnostic character can split a group). Lumps interbreeding populations that share a recent ancestor.

Also commonly used: ECOLOGICAL species concept (occupying same niche) and GENOTYPIC CLUSTER (Mallet's, populations form clusters in genotype space).

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Species delimitation matters for taxonomy, conservation prioritization, and biodiversity counting. Different concepts give different counts; the choice has political/legal consequences.

⚠ TRAP: Asking 'what is the right species concept' is the wrong question. Each concept is a tool optimized for different data.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#7] Mayr's Biological Species Concept (BSC) defines a species as:
  A. A group of actually or potentially interbreeding natural populations
  B. Any group of organisms occupying the same niche.
  C. A group of organisms with the same morphology.
  D. The smallest monophyletic group identifiable by shared derived characters.
→ Answer: A

[Final-A · MC#29] Which of the following groups is the Biological Species Concept LEAST well suited to?
  A. Sexual birds.
  B. Sexual mammals.
  C. Asexual bacteria.
  D. Sexual amphibians.
→ Answer: C

cards.term: PRE before zygote (HTBMG), POST after (ISB)
cards.definition:
🐦 REPRODUCTIVE ISOLATION MECHANISMS

📌 The phrase: Barriers between species act either BEFORE or AFTER fertilization. Each timing has its own set of mechanisms.

◆ PRE-ZYGOTIC (act before fertilization):
  H — HABITAT isolation (different microhabitats; rarely encounter each other)
  T — TEMPORAL isolation (breed at different times of year/day)
  B — BEHAVIORAL isolation (different courtship signals; mates ignore each other)
  M — MECHANICAL isolation (genitalia don't fit; flower structure mismatch)
  G — GAMETIC isolation (sperm can't fertilize egg; pollen rejected)

◆ POST-ZYGOTIC (act after fertilization):
  I — hybrid INVIABILITY (zygote dies; F1 doesn't develop)
  S — hybrid STERILITY (mules! horse × donkey produces healthy but sterile offspring)
  B — F2 BREAKDOWN (hybrids fertile but their offspring weak/sterile)

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: PRE-zygotic barriers are CHEAPER (don't waste a gamete). Selection can REINFORCE prezygotic barriers when hybrids are unfit — that's the reinforcement mechanism that completes speciation.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Mules (horse × donkey) are healthy but sterile = postzygotic STERILITY. Two cricket species singing at different temperatures = HABITAT/temporal mix. Pollen-pistil incompatibility in plants = GAMETIC.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-B · MC#11] Two related fly species court at different times of day, so they rarely encounter each other. This is best classified as:
  A. Prezygotic isolation — temporal.
  B. Prezygotic isolation — mechanical.
  C. Postzygotic isolation — hybrid sterility.
  D. Postzygotic isolation — hybrid breakdown.
→ Answer: A

[Final-B · MC#16] Horses and donkeys mate and produce viable offspring (mules), but mules are sterile. This is best classified as:
  A. Prezygotic isolation — behavioral.
  B. Postzygotic isolation — hybrid sterility.
  C. Postzygotic isolation — hybrid inviability.
  D. Prezygotic isolation — gametic.
→ Answer: B

cards.term: ASP — Allopatric Apart, Sympatric Same place, Parapatric Partly overlap
cards.definition:
🐦 THE 3 GEOGRAPHIC MODES OF SPECIATION

📌 The phrase: How populations diverge into separate species, classified by spatial relationship.

◆ ALLOPATRIC — populations separated by a geographic barrier (mountain, river, sea-level change). No gene flow → divergence accumulates → reproductive isolation evolves. THE MOST COMMON mode of speciation. Two flavors: vicariance (barrier appears) and peripatric (small population isolated at edge).
◆ SYMPATRIC — populations diverge in the SAME place, with potential gene flow. Hard to do; gene flow normally collapses divergence. Mechanisms: polyploidy in plants (instant), host-race shifts in insects, strong disruptive selection + assortative mating, sexual selection on ornament/preference.
◆ PARAPATRIC — populations diverge along an environmental gradient with adjacent ranges and partial overlap. Selection across the gradient + limited gene flow → reproductive isolation in the contact zone.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Mode of speciation determines what genes diverge first, how stable the new species is, and how easily hybrid zones form.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Allopatric — Galápagos finches diverged on different islands. Sympatric — apple maggot fly (Rhagoletis pomonella) shifted from native hawthorn to introduced apple in 1850s, now diverging in same orchards. Parapatric — Anthoxanthum grass evolves heavy-metal tolerance on mine tailings adjacent to normal soil.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#16] Two populations of squirrels are separated when a mountain range rises between them. Over time, they diverge and become reproductively incompatible. This is:
  A. Allopatric speciation
  B. Sympatric speciation.
  C. Peripatric speciation only.
  D. Parapatric speciation.
→ Answer: A

[Final-D · MC#6] Sympatric speciation is most common in plants because of which mechanism?
  A. Plants have shorter generation times.
  B. Polyploidy — whole-genome duplication can immediately produce a reproductively isolated lineage in a single generation.
  C. Plants have higher mutation rates than animals.
  D. Plants are more mobile than animals.
→ Answer: B

cards.term: Polyploidy: Auto = Self-doubling, Allo = Hybrid + doubling
cards.definition:
🐦 INSTANT SPECIATION VIA WHOLE-GENOME DUPLICATION

📌 The phrase: Polyploidy = having more than 2 sets of chromosomes (3n, 4n, etc.). Two ways to get there.

◆ AUTOPOLYPLOIDY — chromosome number doubles within a single species (failed meiosis, unreduced gametes). All chromosomes from same ancestor.
◆ ALLOPOLYPLOIDY — hybridization between two species, then chromosome doubling restores fertility (each chromosome now has a homolog). Common in plants.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Polyploidy can produce instant speciation in ONE generation — polyploid offspring are reproductively isolated from diploid parents (different chromosome counts → sterile hybrids). The fastest mode of speciation known. Common in plants (~70% of flowering plants have polyploidy in their history); rarer in animals.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) is hexaploid (6n) — formed by repeated allopolyploidy among ancestral wheat species. Strawberries are octoploid. Many crop species' large fruit/seed traits are polyploidy-driven.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#6] Sympatric speciation is most common in plants because of which mechanism?
  A. Plants have shorter generation times.
  B. Polyploidy — whole-genome duplication can immediately produce a reproductively isolated lineage in a single generation.
  C. Plants have higher mutation rates than animals.
  D. Plants are more mobile than animals.
→ Answer: B

[Final-C · MC#10] Reinforcement of speciation occurs when:
  A. Geographic isolation alone completes speciation.
  B. Two species that have come back into secondary contact evolve stronger prezygotic isolation
  C. Species independently evolve similar traits in different regions.
  D. Polyploidy doubles chromosome counts — that's polyploidy, a mode of sympatric
→ Answer: B

cards.term: Reinforcement strengthens prezygotic walls
cards.definition:
🐦 REINFORCEMENT — COMPLETING SPECIATION

📌 The phrase: When two diverged populations come back into contact and produce unfit hybrids, selection favors INDIVIDUALS THAT AVOID HYBRIDIZING. Prezygotic barriers tighten — speciation completes.

◆ Two populations diverge in allopatry → secondary contact → hybrids form but have low fitness (postzygotic isolation already exists)
◆ Individuals choosing the wrong species waste reproductive effort → strong selection AGAINST hybridizing
◆ Result: PRE-ZYGOTIC barriers strengthen (mate preference shifts, courtship signals diverge further) — reproductive isolation locks in.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Reinforcement converts incipient species (some hybridization, fertile-ish hybrids) into fully separate species. It's the mechanism that 'finishes' speciation when populations meet again.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Pied + collared flycatchers in central Europe — where they overlap, female preferences for own-species males are STRONGER than where each species lives alone. Classic reinforcement signature.

⚠ TRAP: Reinforcement only works if some postzygotic isolation already exists. Otherwise hybrids are fine and there's no selection against mismating.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-C · MC#10] Reinforcement of speciation occurs when:
  A. Geographic isolation alone completes speciation.
  B. Two species that have come back into secondary contact evolve stronger prezygotic isolation
  C. Species independently evolve similar traits in different regions.
  D. Polyploidy doubles chromosome counts — that's polyploidy, a mode of sympatric
→ Answer: B

[Final-D · MC#29] A hybrid zone exists where two species' ranges overlap and they interbreed, producing low-fitness hybrids. Does the existence of this hybrid zone disprove the species' status under the BSC?
