  A. Cannot be determined without additional evidence.
  B. Yes — only completely non-interbreeding populations are species.
  C. No — if hybrids have reduced fitness, gene flow remains limited
  D. Yes — any interbreeding means they are the same species.
→ Answer: C

cards.term: Dispersal Jumps barriers, Vicariance Splits ranges
cards.definition:
🗺️ TWO MODES OF BIOGEOGRAPHIC RANGE FORMATION

📌 The phrase: Two ways species end up where they are.

◆ DISPERSAL — active movement across a pre-existing barrier. The barrier was always there; the organism crossed it. Examples: Hawaiian birds (ancestors flew/blew across ocean), Galápagos finches (founders dispersed from mainland).
◆ VICARIANCE — barrier APPEARS, splitting an existing range. Continental drift, mountain uplift, sea-level change, river formation. The species didn't move; the world moved around it. Examples: marsupials in Australia + South America (split as Gondwana broke up), velvet worms (Onychophora) — fragmented ancient distribution.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Same modern distribution can result from either mechanism, but they have very different evolutionary timing and predictions. Dispersal is unpredictable (rare events); vicariance produces predictable congruent patterns across many taxa simultaneously.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Wallace Line (between Bali and Lombok) — placental mammals on the Asian side, marsupials on the Australian side. Reflects deep history when Australia was isolated; the line is a biogeographic relic of vicariance.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#20] Closely related plant lineages on South America and Africa share an ancestor that lived ~120 MYA. The most likely explanation is:
  A. Convergent evolution producing similar plants.
  B. Long-distance bird-mediated seed transport at the species' age.
  C. Recent dispersal across the Atlantic Ocean.
  D. Vicariance — the lineage was once continuous on Gondwana before South America and Africa separated.
→ Answer: D

[Final-D · MC#2] Two related lizard species occur on different sides of a mountain range that uplifted ~10 MYA. The lizards' lineage split also dates to ~10 MYA. This pattern most likely reflects:
  A. Convergent evolution — convergent evolution doesn't speak to phylogenetic split
  B. Dispersal — the lizards crossed the mountain after it formed.
  C. Drift in a small population — drift doesn't produce a coordinated split timed
  D. Vicariance — the rising mountain split a previously continuous population.
→ Answer: D

cards.term: Wallace Line: Asia ends, Australia begins
cards.definition:
🗺️ WALLACE'S LINE — A BIOGEOGRAPHIC FAULT

📌 The phrase: A faunal divide between Bali and Lombok (Indonesia) — only ~35 km wide, but separates dramatically different mammal faunas.

◆ Asian side (Bali) — placental mammals: tigers, monkeys, elephants in deeper history
◆ Australian side (Lombok) — marsupials and monotremes

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Discovered by Alfred Russel Wallace during the Malay Archipelago expedition (1854-1862) — the same trip during which he conceived natural selection. The line reveals deep history: even though the islands are now close together, they sit on different continental shelves that were separate during low sea-level glacial periods. Animals that couldn't cross the deep-water Lombok Strait stayed on their side.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Sumatra and Java are on the Sunda Shelf (Asian fauna). Sulawesi, Lombok, and east are on the Sahul/Australian side. Birds and bats can sometimes cross the line; non-flying terrestrial mammals largely cannot.

📖 STORY: Wallace also published the 1858 manuscript with Darwin on natural selection. The Wallace Line is a permanent monument to his fieldwork.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-C · MC#30] The Wallace Line is:
  A. A line on a phylogenetic tree separating chordates from arthropods.
  B. A faunal boundary in the Indonesian archipelago that separates Asian and Australasian biotas
  C. A genetic marker used to date the human-chimpanzee split.
  D. The boundary of Wallace's voyage on the HMS Beagle.
→ Answer: B

[Final-A · MC#20] Closely related plant lineages on South America and Africa share an ancestor that lived ~120 MYA. The most likely explanation is:
  A. Convergent evolution producing similar plants.
  B. Long-distance bird-mediated seed transport at the species' age.
  C. Recent dispersal across the Atlantic Ocean.
  D. Vicariance — the lineage was once continuous on Gondwana before South America and Africa separated.
→ Answer: D

cards.term: Adaptive Radiation: One Ancestor, Many Niches
cards.definition:
🗺️ ADAPTIVE RADIATION — RAPID DIVERGENCE INTO MANY FORMS

📌 The phrase: A single ancestral species rapidly diversifies into many descendant species occupying different ecological niches.

◆ Triggers — KEY INNOVATION (a new trait that enables exploitation of new resources/habitats) + OPEN NICHE SPACE (post-extinction or new island/lake/continent)

📐 CLASSIC CASES TO MEMORIZE:
→ Hawaiian honeycreepers — different beak shapes for different foods (nectar, seeds, insects)
→ Galápagos finches — Darwin's classic, 14 species from one mainland ancestor
→ African Rift Lake cichlid fishes — hundreds of species in single lakes (Victoria, Tanganyika, Malawi); jaw morphology diverged repeatedly
→ Caribbean Anolis lizards — same ECOMORPH categories (twig, trunk-ground, crown-giant, twig dwarf) evolved independently on each island = parallel adaptive radiation

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Adaptive radiation is responsible for much of the world's biological diversity. It demonstrates that evolution can be FAST when conditions allow — refutes the assumption that change requires millions of years.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Hawaiian silverswords — 28 species of plants from a single tarweed ancestor that arrived ~5 MYA. Forms range from tall trees to ground rosettes. All within 5 MY.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#22] Which condition most strongly favors adaptive radiation?
  A. Genetic drift in a single population.
  B. Open ecological space (e.g.
  C. High predation pressure.
  D. A stable, fully occupied ecosystem.
→ Answer: B

[Final-B · MC#26] Why did mammals undergo a major adaptive radiation after the K-Pg extinction?
  A. Mammals appeared for the first time after the K-Pg.
  B. Mammals were not affected by the asteroid impact.
  C. Mammals had higher mutation rates after the extinction.
  D. Mammals had been small and ecologically restricted
→ Answer: D

cards.term: Sahel → Ardi → Australo → Habilis → Erectus → Sapiens
cards.definition:
🧠 THE HOMININ LINEAGE

📌 The phrase: Major hominin genera/species in rough chronological order. 7 MYA → present.

◆ SAHELANTHROPUS tchadensis (~7 MYA, Chad) — earliest plausible hominin. Skull shows features hinting at bipedalism.
◆ ARDIPITHECUS ramidus ('Ardi,' ~4.4 MYA, Ethiopia) — partial bipedalism but climbing-adapted feet. Shows the transition.
◆ AUSTRALOPITHECUS (4-2 MYA) — fully bipedal with ape-sized brains. Multiple species. Includes Lucy (A. afarensis, 3.2 MYA).
◆ HOMO HABILIS (~2.4-1.4 MYA) — first stone tools (Oldowan). Brain enlargement begins.
◆ HOMO ERECTUS (~1.9 MYA - 110 KYA) — first to leave Africa (~1.8 MYA). Larger brain, fire use, Acheulean tools.
◆ HOMO SAPIENS (~300 KYA - present) — modern humans. Originated in Africa, dispersed ~60-70 KYA.

Also: H. neanderthalensis (~400-40 KYA, Europe/W Asia) and Denisovans — sister groups that interbred with sapiens.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Reveals that human evolution is BUSHY, not linear. Multiple hominin species coexisted at any given time. We're the only one left.

🔬 EXAMPLE: As recently as 40 KYA, Homo sapiens, Neanderthals, Denisovans, Homo floresiensis ('hobbit'), and possibly Homo luzonensis all coexisted. The 'last man standing' is not the rule of evolution but a recent oddity.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#21] 'Lucy' is a famous specimen of which species?
  A. Australopithecus afarensis
  B. Sahelanthropus tchadensis
  C. Homo neanderthalensis
  D. Homo erectus
→ Answer: A

[Final-B · MC#29] Bipedal locomotion in the hominin lineage began approximately:
  A. 6–7 million years ago
  B. 200,000 years ago
  C. 100 million years ago
  D. 1 million years ago
→ Answer: A

cards.term: Bipedalism FIRST, Big Brain LATER
cards.definition:
🧠 MOSAIC HUMAN EVOLUTION

📌 The phrase: The hallmark traits of humans didn't all evolve at once. Bipedalism appeared 4-7 MYA; brain enlargement didn't take off until ~2 MYA in genus Homo.

◆ BIPEDALISM came first — Lucy (A. afarensis, 3.2 MYA) walked upright but had a chimp-sized brain (~400 cc). Foot bones, pelvis, and Laetoli footprints (~3.6 MYA) are all clear evidence.
◆ STONE TOOLS came next (~2.6 MYA, Oldowan)
◆ BIG BRAIN expansion accelerated in genus Homo — H. habilis ~600 cc, H. erectus ~900 cc, H. sapiens ~1350 cc.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: This 'mosaic evolution' pattern was unsettled until Lucy was found (1974). Before Lucy, many assumed brain expansion drove bipedalism. Lucy proved the opposite: bipedalism comes first, then brain.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Lucy's pelvis is human-like (bipedal); her skull is ape-like (small brain). The mismatch was the smoking gun for mosaic evolution.

📖 STORY: Lucy (AL 288-1) was found by Donald Johanson in Hadar, Ethiopia, on 24 November 1974. Named after 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds' which played at the celebration camp. ~40% of her skeleton was preserved.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-B · MC#29] Bipedal locomotion in the hominin lineage began approximately:
  A. 6–7 million years ago
  B. 200,000 years ago
  C. 100 million years ago
  D. 1 million years ago
→ Answer: A

[Final-A · MC#21] 'Lucy' is a famous specimen of which species?
  A. Australopithecus afarensis
  B. Sahelanthropus tchadensis
  C. Homo neanderthalensis
  D. Homo erectus
→ Answer: A

cards.term: Out-of-Africa Twice — Erectus 1.8 MYA, Sapiens 60-70 KYA
cards.definition:
🧠 THE TWO MAJOR HOMININ DISPERSALS

📌 The phrase: Africa is the source. Two major waves of hominins dispersed out of it.

◆ FIRST WAVE — Homo erectus, ~1.8 MYA. Spread to Asia (Dmanisi in Georgia, Java, China) and possibly Europe. Was the first hominin to leave Africa.
◆ SECOND WAVE — Homo sapiens, ~60-70 KYA. Spread out of Africa (after smaller earlier excursions); colonized Eurasia, Australia (~50 KYA), Americas (~20-15 KYA). Replaced or assimilated other hominin species.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: This 'Out-of-Africa' model is supported by both fossils and genetics. African populations have the most genetic diversity (oldest source), while non-African populations carry a SUBSET of African variation — characteristic of a founder/serial-bottleneck pattern.

📐 EVIDENCE:
→ All non-African Y-chromosome and mitochondrial lineages nest within African ones
→ Genetic diversity decreases with distance from Africa
→ Fossil evidence shows H. sapiens in Africa by 300 KYA, in Levant by ~100 KYA, widespread in Eurasia by 50 KYA

⚠ TRAP: 'Multiregional' models (parallel evolution from H. erectus in different continents) have been mostly rejected by genetic evidence, though some interbreeding (with Neanderthals/Denisovans) DID occur after the OoA dispersal.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#3] Which hominin species was the FIRST to disperse out of Africa?
  A. Australopithecus afarensis
  B. Homo erectus
  C. Homo sapiens
  D. Homo neanderthalensis
→ Answer: B

[Final-C · MC#13] Modern non-African humans typically carry approximately what fraction of Neanderthal-derived DNA?
  A. 20–30%
  B. 50%
  C. 1–4%
  D. 0%
→ Answer: C

cards.term: Non-Africans = 1-4% Neanderthal; Asians/Oceanians + Denisovan
cards.definition:
🧠 INTROGRESSION FROM ARCHAIC HUMANS

📌 The phrase: Modern humans interbred with Neanderthals and Denisovans during the Out-of-Africa dispersal. Their genes live on in non-African genomes.

◆ NEANDERTHAL DNA — non-Africans carry ~1-4% Neanderthal ancestry. From interbreeding ~50-60 KYA in the Middle East / Eurasia. Some segments are functional and under selection (immunity, skin, hair).
◆ DENISOVAN DNA — Asians, Oceanians, Native Americans carry additional Denisovan ancestry (highest in Melanesians, ~3-6%). From interbreeding events in Asia. EPAS1 variant from Denisovans helps Tibetans tolerate high altitude.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Modern humans are not a 'pure' lineage — we are a mosaic. Some archaic alleles confer adaptive benefits (altitude, immunity); others may contribute to disease risk (Type 2 diabetes, Crohn's). Reshapes how we think about 'us' vs 'them' in hominin evolution.

📐 KEY DISCOVERIES:
→ Neanderthal genome sequenced 2010 (Pääbo lab) — confirmed introgression
→ Denisova cave (Siberia, 2010) — single finger bone yielded a previously unknown hominin lineage
→ Selected genes: BNC2 (skin), EPAS1 (altitude), STAT2 (immunity)

📖 STORY: Svante Pääbo won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for sequencing the Neanderthal genome and discovering Denisovans.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-C · MC#13] Modern non-African humans typically carry approximately what fraction of Neanderthal-derived DNA?
  A. 20–30%
  B. 50%
  C. 1–4%
  D. 0%
→ Answer: C

[Final-D · MC#3] Which hominin species was the FIRST to disperse out of Africa?
  A. Australopithecus afarensis
  B. Homo erectus
  C. Homo sapiens
  D. Homo neanderthalensis
→ Answer: B

cards.term: Tools: Oldowan → Acheulean → Mousterian → Upper Paleolithic
cards.definition:
🧠 STONE TOOL TRADITIONS — A 2.6 MY TIMELINE

📌 The phrase: Four major stone-tool cultures, in chronological order, each associated with specific hominin makers.

◆ OLDOWAN (~2.6 MYA - 1.7 MYA) — H. habilis. Simple flakes struck from cobbles. First evidence of cultural transmission.
◆ ACHEULEAN (~1.7 MYA - 200 KYA) — H. erectus. Symmetric, bifacial 'hand-axes' — requires planning and shaping the whole tool.
◆ MOUSTERIAN (~300 KYA - 30 KYA) — Neanderthals primarily. Prepared-core technique (Levallois): preshape a core to produce flakes of predetermined shape. Hafting (attaching points to handles).
◆ UPPER PALEOLITHIC (~50 KYA - 10 KYA) — H. sapiens. Blade technology, bone/antler tools, projectile points, art (cave paintings, figurines), personal ornaments.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Tools are the OBJECTIVE record of cognitive evolution. Each tradition shows incremental advances in:
→ Planning depth (more steps before final tool)
→ Material variety (stone, bone, ivory, antler)
→ Symbolic thinking (art appears in Upper Paleo)
→ Cumulative culture (each generation builds on the last)

🔬 EXAMPLE: Lascaux cave paintings (~17 KYA) — stunning Upper Paleolithic art. Acheulean hand-axes have been found from Africa to Europe to India, used by H. erectus for ~1.5 MY with little change.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#3] Which hominin species was the FIRST to disperse out of Africa?
  A. Australopithecus afarensis
  B. Homo erectus
  C. Homo sapiens
  D. Homo neanderthalensis
→ Answer: B

[Final-B · MC#29] Bipedal locomotion in the hominin lineage began approximately:
  A. 6–7 million years ago
  B. 200,000 years ago
  C. 100 million years ago
  D. 1 million years ago
→ Answer: A

cards.term: Bugs Evolve Faster Than We Make Drugs
cards.definition:
💊 ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE

📌 The phrase: Microbial generations are short and population sizes are huge — bacteria can evolve resistance within years, while developing new antibiotics takes a decade or more.

◆ MECHANISM — when antibiotics are used, susceptible bacteria die; rare resistant variants survive and reproduce. After a few generations, the resistant variant dominates. Pure directional selection.
◆ RESISTANCE GENES SPREAD — horizontally via plasmids, transposons, phages — between species. A resistance gene in E. coli can jump to Salmonella.
◆ HUMAN BEHAVIORS THAT SELECT — overprescription, incomplete antibiotic courses, agricultural use (livestock feed), poor sanitation in hospitals.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: A direct, observable, modern-day evolutionary process with massive medical consequences. MRSA, multi-drug-resistant TB, and carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE) are real and growing public health threats. Without intervention, common infections may become untreatable.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Methicillin-resistant Staph aureus (MRSA) — first identified in 1961, ~2 years after methicillin's introduction. Now globally widespread. Vancomycin-resistant strains follow each new last-line antibiotic.

⚠ TRAP: Stopping antibiotics early ('I feel better') leaves partially-resistant bacteria behind to reproduce. Always finish the prescribed course.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#9] Hospitals that heavily use a particular antibiotic see rising rates of resistance to that antibiotic. Which evolutionary mechanism is most directly responsible?
  A. Natural selection on rare resistant mutants that arise independently of the antibiotic.
  B. Lamarckian inheritance — bacteria acquire resistance from exposure and pass it to offspring.
  C. Mutation rate increases when antibiotics are present, generating resistance on demand.
  D. Genetic drift — random change in a small bacterial population.
→ Answer: A

[Final-D · MC#5] Antibiotic resistance in bacteria is a textbook example of natural selection because:
  A. Resistance is acquired during a bacterium's lifetime and passed via cell division.
  B. Antibiotics induce mutations toward resistance.
  C. Resistance mutations occur randomly
  D. Bacteria deliberately evolve resistance.
→ Answer: C

cards.term: Virulence Trade-off: Transmission Trumps Tameness
cards.definition:
💊 PATHOGEN VIRULENCE EVOLVES WITH TRANSMISSION MODE

📌 The phrase: How deadly a pathogen 'should' be depends on how it spreads. Trade-off between killing the host and getting transmitted.

◆ DIRECT-CONTACT TRANSMISSION (host needs to walk around to infect others) → selection favors LOW virulence. Common cold rarely kills you because dead people don't sneeze on others.
◆ VECTOR-BORNE / WATERBORNE TRANSMISSION (host doesn't need to be mobile) → selection allows HIGH virulence. Cholera (waterborne), malaria (mosquito-borne), Yersinia pestis (flea-borne) — can be deadly because transmission doesn't require host activity.
◆ NOSOCOMIAL (hospital-acquired) — staff move pathogens, not patients → high virulence often evolves.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Predicts which pathogens will be deadly vs mild based on biology, not malice. Public-health interventions that change transmission (clean water, mosquito nets) can EVOLUTIONARILY select for less virulent strains over time.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Myxoma virus released into Australian rabbits in 1950 was initially ~99.5% lethal. Within years, strains of MODERATE virulence dominated — they kept hosts alive long enough to be bitten by transmitting mosquitoes. Classic in-progress evolution of virulence.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#15] Why does the common cold (respiratory, directly transmitted) tend to evolve toward MILDER virulence, while cholera (waterborne) does not face the same pressure?
  A. The common cold has higher mutation rates.
  B. Cholera bacteria are larger than cold viruses.
  C. Directly transmitted pathogens need a healthy, mobile host to spread
  D. The common cold evolved earlier than cholera.
→ Answer: C

[Final-B · MC#17] Why does aggressive chemotherapy that initially shrinks a tumor often lead to relapse with drug-resistant cancer?
  A. Chemotherapy is a strong selective pressure
  B. Chemotherapy causes new cancer mutations.
  C. The drug stops working after a few weeks regardless.
  D. Cancers learn from chemotherapy.
→ Answer: A

cards.term: Mismatch Hypothesis: Stone-Age Genes in Space-Age World
cards.definition:
💊 EVOLUTIONARY MISMATCH IN MODERN HEALTH

📌 The phrase: Many modern diseases reflect adaptations to ANCESTRAL environments that are out of sync with our current ones.

◆ DIET — we evolved to crave sweet/fatty foods because they were rare and nutritionally valuable on the savanna. Now sugar and fat are everywhere → obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease.
◆ ACTIVITY — evolved for daily physical work; now sedentary → metabolic syndrome.
◆ SUNLIGHT/SLEEP — evolved with sunrise/sunset; now screens disrupt circadian rhythms → sleep disorders, depression.
◆ MICROBIAL EXPOSURE — evolved with diverse microbiota; modern hygiene reduces exposure → autoimmune disease (hygiene hypothesis), allergies.
◆ SOCIAL — evolved in groups of ~150; now urban anonymity → loneliness, anxiety, depression.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Many 'diseases of civilization' aren't dysfunctions — they're our evolved physiology working as designed in the wrong environment. Public health interventions inspired by this framework target environments, not just symptoms.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Sickle-cell allele was a balanced polymorphism advantage in malaria zones; today, in malaria-free regions with modern medicine, sickle-cell anemia is just a costly disease. Lactase persistence — in adults — is a recent evolutionary change in dairying populations; people without it suffer in dairy-rich societies (lactose intolerance).

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#10] Type 2 diabetes is rare in traditional hunter-gatherer populations and prevalent in industrialized populations. Which evolutionary explanation best fits?
  A. Mismatch — traits adaptive in ancestral environments (efficient fat storage
  B. Industrialized populations have weaker immune systems.
  C. Hunter-gatherers have higher mutation rates that prevent diabetes.
  D. Hunter-gatherers do not have the genes for diabetes.
→ Answer: A

[Final-C · MC#12] Evolutionary medicine differs from conventional medicine primarily by:
  A. Asking WHY (in evolutionary terms) bodies are vulnerable to disease
  B. Using evolutionary concepts to oppose vaccination and antibiotics.
  C. Focusing only on infectious disease — evolutionary medicine spans infectious disease,
  D. Replacing modern medical practice with paleolithic remedies.
→ Answer: A

cards.term: Antagonistic Pleiotropy = Why we age
cards.definition:
💊 WILLIAMS'S TRADE-OFF THEORY OF SENESCENCE

📌 The phrase: Some genes are GOOD when you're young and BAD when you're old. Selection favors them anyway because the early benefit outweighs the late cost.

◆ SELECTION SHADOW — selection is strongest on traits expressed early in life (when most carriers are still alive and reproducing) and weakest on late-life traits (most carriers have already reproduced or died). Late-life consequences are 'invisible' to selection.
◆ ANTAGONISTIC PLEIOTROPY — a single gene with multiple effects (pleiotropy), some good (early-life advantage) and some bad (late-life cost). Net selection is positive because the early benefit outweighs the late cost.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Aging isn't a 'design failure' — it's an unavoidable consequence of how selection works. Many age-related diseases (cancer, cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration) may have origins in genes that helped you survive to reproduction.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Testosterone signaling — boosts strength, libido, fertility in young males but raises prostate cancer risk in older ones. p53 'guardian of the genome' — suppresses tumors but also limits stem-cell renewal, contributing to age-related decline. BRCA1/2 — DNA repair benefits early; deficient repair increases late-life cancer risk in carriers.

⚠ TRAP: Antagonistic pleiotropy is one of THREE evolutionary aging theories (Mutation Accumulation, Antagonistic Pleiotropy, Disposable Soma). They're not mutually exclusive — all probably contribute.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#5] Most cancers occur in older individuals. From an evolutionary perspective, why has selection failed to eliminate cancer susceptibility?
  A. Cancer is contagious in some species.
  B. Cancer was unknown in ancestral populations.
  C. All organisms have an upper age limit.
  D. Selection's strength declines with age
→ Answer: D

[Final-C · MC#20] Medawar's mutation accumulation theory of aging proposes that:
  A. Each species has a fixed number of cell divisions.
  B. Mutations are more common in older individuals.
  C. Late-acting deleterious mutations escape selection and accumulate in the gene pool
  D. Aging is caused by accumulation of toxins.
→ Answer: C

cards.term: AS Heterozygote-Advantage in malaria zone
cards.definition:
🔬 SICKLE-CELL: BALANCED POLYMORPHISM

📌 The phrase: The S allele for sickle hemoglobin is maintained at high frequency in malaria zones because the heterozygote (AS) outperforms BOTH homozygotes.

◆ AA (normal) — vulnerable to malaria. Higher mortality in malaria zones.
◆ AS (heterozygote) — RESISTANT to malaria (sickle trait misshapes infected RBCs, killing the parasite). Mostly healthy.
◆ SS (homozygous sickle) — sickle-cell anemia. Severely anemic; reduced fitness even with modern medicine.

📐 THE BALANCE: Selection against AA (from malaria) and selection against SS (from anemia) keeps the S allele at moderate frequency where AS heterozygotes dominate. Without malaria, S would be eliminated. Without sickle-cell disease, S would fix.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: This is the textbook example of OVERDOMINANCE / HETEROZYGOTE ADVANTAGE — a mechanism that maintains genetic polymorphism. Also illustrates that an allele can be 'beneficial' in some genotypes and lethal in others.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Equilibrium S frequency in malarial West Africa ~0.10-0.15. After populations migrate out of malaria zones (e.g., African-American populations), selection no longer favors AS — frequency drifts down over generations.

⚠ TRAP: AS individuals do experience some symptoms under extreme conditions (severe dehydration, high altitude). Not 'completely fine' — just much fitter than AA in malaria zones.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-C · MC#11] A population has p = 0.4 (allele A) and q = 0.6 (allele a). Hardy-Weinberg expects 32% heterozygotes (2pq = 0.48 → 48%, sorry let me recompute: 2 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 0.48 = 48%). The population is observed to have only 20% heterozygotes. Which mechanism best explains this deviation?
  A. Inbreeding or population subdivision
  B. Strong selection against the AA homozygote
  C. Heterozygote advantage (overdominance)
  D. Recent admixture between populations
→ Answer: A

[Final-A · MC#23] Which of the following is NOT one of the five assumptions of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
  A. Random mating
  B. Infinite population size
  C. Equal allele frequencies
  D. No mutation
→ Answer: C

cards.term: Tame in 50 Generations brings Floppy ears, Spots, Curly tails
cards.definition:
🔬 BELYAEV'S FOX EXPERIMENT — DOMESTICATION SYNDROME

📌 The phrase: Selecting only for tameness in silver foxes produced an entire suite of unrelated 'domestic' traits in ~50 generations.

◆ Started 1959 by Soviet geneticist Dmitry Belyaev (Novosibirsk).
◆ Selected ONLY for tameness (foxes that approached humans without fear/aggression).
◆ After ~30-50 generations, foxes showed:
  → Tame, dog-like behavior
  → FLOPPY EARS
  → COAT SPOTS / piebald patterns
  → CURLY TAILS
  → Shorter snouts
  → Earlier sexual maturity
  → Lower stress hormone levels

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: This is THE classic demonstration of:
→ How fast selection can produce coordinated change
→ PLEIOTROPY — selecting on one trait drags many others along (probably via neural-crest-cell development pathways shared by ear cartilage, pigment cells, adrenal stress response)
→ Why all domesticated mammals (dogs, cattle, pigs, horses) share similar 'domestication syndrome' features

🔬 EXAMPLE: Dogs vs wolves — same suite of changes from selection on tameness. Belyaev's foxes are essentially recapitulating wolf-to-dog domestication in real time.

📖 STORY: The experiment continues today (Lyudmila Trut runs it). Tame foxes are sometimes sold as pets; aggressive foxes (from a parallel selection line) are also bred for comparison.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#3] On Ram Mountain, bighorn sheep were heavily trophy-hunted for large-horned males. Over decades, average horn size in the population DECREASED. The most likely cause is:
  A. Selective hunting of large-horned individuals removed those phenotypes from the breeding pool
  B. Sheep with large horns voluntarily hid them.
  C. Random drift in a large population.
  D. Climate change shrank horns.
→ Answer: A

[Final-A · MC#17] Which of the following best defines biological evolution?
  A. An individual organism becoming better adapted over its lifetime.
  B. Change in the heritable traits of a population across generations.
  C. Progressive improvement of organisms toward greater complexity.
  D. Random variation among individuals within a single generation.
→ Answer: B

cards.term: Soot Selects Black, Clean returns to Pepper
cards.definition:
🔬 PEPPERED MOTHS — INDUSTRIAL MELANISM

📌 The phrase: The peppered moth (Biston betularia) shifted from light to dark coloration during the Industrial Revolution as soot-darkened tree bark made dark moths better camouflaged.

◆ PRE-INDUSTRIAL — light, peppered (typica) form was common; melanic (carbonaria) form was rare (~<1%).
◆ INDUSTRIAL ERA (mid-1800s onward) — coal soot blackened tree bark and lichen-killed surfaces. Light moths became visible to bird predators on dark trunks. Dark melanic form rose to ~98% near industrial centers.
◆ POST-CLEAN-AIR-ACT (1956 UK) — pollution decreased, lichens returned, tree bark lightened. Frequencies REVERSED — peppered form now dominant again.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Real-time documentation of:
→ Directional natural selection in action
→ Predation as the selective agent
→ Reversibility of selection when environment changes

🔬 EXAMPLE: Bernard Kettlewell's classic 1950s field experiments — released marked moths in polluted Birmingham vs clean Dorset; recapture rates confirmed differential predation. The story is a textbook staple of evolution-by-natural-selection.

⚠ TRAP: Some methodological criticism of Kettlewell's specific protocols was made in the 1990s, but subsequent more rigorous studies (Majerus 2002-2007) confirmed the basic finding — bird predation drives the directional shift.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#26] Why did the dark (melanic) form of Biston betularia rise to dominance in industrial regions of England?
  A. Polluted air directly killed light-colored moths through respiratory toxicity.
  B. Bird predators were more likely to spot light moths against soot-darkened tree trunks
  C. Pollution induced melanism in moths during their lifetime.
  D. Moths actively chose darker resting sites in polluted areas.
→ Answer: B

[Final-B · MC#13] After the UK's Clean Air Act reduced pollution, peppered moth populations shifted back toward the light morph. This best illustrates:
  A. Selection direction can reverse when the environment changes.
  B. Mutations had to occur to produce the light morph.
  C. Genetic drift is more powerful than selection.
  D. Selection direction is fixed once a trait evolves.
→ Answer: A

cards.term: Dry Drives Deep beaks, Wet welcomes Wee beaks
cards.definition:
🔬 GRANTS' GALÁPAGOS FINCHES — SELECTION IN REAL TIME

📌 The phrase: Beak morphology of Geospiza fortis (medium ground finch) tracks rainfall and seed availability across years — observed directional selection visible within single seasons.

◆ DRY YEAR (1977 drought) — soft small seeds depleted first. Only LARGE, HARD SEEDS remain. Birds with deeper, stronger beaks survive (can crack tough seeds). Mean beak depth INCREASES the next generation.
◆ WET YEAR (1983 El Niño) — abundance of soft small seeds. Smaller beaks now efficient. Mean beak depth DECREASES in next generation.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Field-documented directional selection at sub-decadal timescales. Demonstrates:
→ Selection responds to environmental change
→ Heritable variation exists in wild populations
→ Evolution by natural selection is FAST when selection is strong
→ Real-time empirical confirmation of Darwinian theory

🔬 EXAMPLE: Peter and Rosemary Grant studied finches on Daphne Major (uninhabited Galápagos islet) for 40+ years. Their data showed:
→ 1977 drought: ~85% of fortis died; survivors had ~5% larger beaks
→ Hybridization with G. scandens after 1983 El Niño introduced new variation
→ A new resident lineage ('Big Bird') arose from a single immigrant in 1981 and became reproductively isolated within 3 generations — possible incipient speciation

📖 STORY: The Grants' work is documented in Jonathan Weiner's 'The Beak of the Finch' (Pulitzer-winning).

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-B · MC#7] After the 1977 drought on Daphne Major, the medium ground finch population shifted toward deeper beaks. The Grants concluded this was natural selection because:
  A. The drought directly caused beaks to grow.
  B. All small-beaked birds happened to die randomly.
  C. Birds physically modified their beaks to deal with hard seeds.
  D. Beak depth was heritable
→ Answer: D

[Final-A · MC#17] Which of the following best defines biological evolution?
  A. An individual organism becoming better adapted over its lifetime.
  B. Change in the heritable traits of a population across generations.
  C. Progressive improvement of organisms toward greater complexity.
  D. Random variation among individuals within a single generation.
→ Answer: B

cards.term: Nothing in Biology Makes Sense Except in the Light of Evolution
cards.definition:
🌍 DOBZHANSKY'S DICTUM — WHY EVOLUTION UNIFIES BIOLOGY

📌 The phrase: Theodosius Dobzhansky (1973) — every observation in biology, from molecular to ecosystem, only makes sense in an evolutionary framework.

◆ Without evolution, biology is a list of disconnected facts (here's a giraffe, here's a virus, here's mitochondria — why?)
◆ With evolution, every fact connects to every other through descent, selection, and shared history.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: This is the pedagogical answer to 'why study evolution?' Every biology class — anatomy, physiology, microbiology, ecology — uses evolution as the explanatory backbone whether stated or not.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Antibiotic resistance, vaccine design, conservation biology, cancer therapy, agricultural breeding — none of these can be done well without evolutionary thinking.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#17] Which of the following best defines biological evolution?
  A. An individual organism becoming better adapted over its lifetime.
  B. Change in the heritable traits of a population across generations.
  C. Progressive improvement of organisms toward greater complexity.
  D. Random variation among individuals within a single generation.
→ Answer: B

[Final-A · MC#18] Why is 'evolution happens' a poor scientific hypothesis even though evolution is well supported?
  A. It is an example of inheritance of acquired characteristics.
  B. It is religious rather than scientific.
  C. It is too broad — it does not specify what observations would prove it wrong.
  D. It is not supported by any evidence.
→ Answer: C

cards.term: Aristotle's Ladder, Linnaeus's Boxes
cards.definition:
📜 PRE-DARWINIAN: GREAT CHAIN OF BEING

📌 The phrase: Before evolution, Western biology held that species are FIXED rungs on a divine ladder — Aristotle's Scala Naturae.

◆ ARISTOTLE'S LADDER — minerals → plants → animals → humans → angels → God. Each species has a fixed place; no change between rungs.
◆ LINNAEUS'S BOXES — Carl Linnaeus (1735) classified species into hierarchical taxa (kingdom→phylum→...→species). Originally meant as descriptions of God's design, NOT as evolutionary trees. Later co-opted by Darwin.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: This worldview was the obstacle Darwin had to overcome. The hierarchy LOOKS like phylogeny but was originally interpreted as a static creation. Linnaeus's nested categories happen to match what evolution predicts — that's why his system survived as the foundation of taxonomy.

⚠ TRAP: Don't confuse the modern Linnaean hierarchy (used in cladistics) with its original fixity-of-species meaning. The boxes are still useful; the philosophical assumption was wrong.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-B · MC#5] Which statement best describes the pre-Darwinian Great Chain of Being?
  A. A fixed hierarchical ladder placing humans at the top and lower forms at the bottom
  B. A theological argument that God created species in series over time.
  C. A geological framework explaining extinction events.
  D. An early evolutionary tree showing common ancestry of organisms.
→ Answer: A

[Final-C · MC#9] How did Charles Lyell's work most directly influence Darwin's theory of natural selection?
  A. Lyell established that Earth was very old
  B. Lyell catalogued the fossils Darwin used in On the Origin of Species.
  C. Lyell discovered the genetic basis of inheritance, providing a mechanism.
  D. Lyell argued that natural selection had been operating on geological scales.
→ Answer: A

cards.term: Hypothesis is a HUNCH, Theory is well-TESTED
cards.definition:
📜 SCIENTIFIC METHOD — HYPOTHESIS vs THEORY

📌 The phrase: 'Theory' in science does NOT mean guess. It means a well-supported explanatory framework that has survived many tests.

◆ HYPOTHESIS — a specific, testable prediction. Tentative. May be wrong.
◆ THEORY — broad, well-tested explanatory framework that ties many hypotheses together. Has predictive power and survives repeated falsification attempts.
◆ LAW — describes a regular pattern, often mathematically (Mendel's laws, gas laws) without explaining why.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: 'Just a theory' is the most common evolution-denial talking point. Theory of evolution sits with theory of gravity, atomic theory, germ theory of disease — all are 'just' theories in the same sense.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Hypothesis = 'this peppered moth's fitness depends on tree-bark color.' Theory = evolution by natural selection (covers thousands of such hypotheses).

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#8] Which of the following is a HYPOTHESIS rather than a scientific theory?
  A. The cell theory — cell theory is
  B. The germ theory of disease.
  C. Antibiotic-resistant strains will increase in frequency in hospitals where antibiotics are heavily used.
  D. Evolution by natural selection.
→ Answer: C

[Final-A · MC#18] Why is 'evolution happens' a poor scientific hypothesis even though evolution is well supported?
  A. It is an example of inheritance of acquired characteristics.
  B. It is religious rather than scientific.
  C. It is too broad — it does not specify what observations would prove it wrong.
  D. It is not supported by any evidence.
→ Answer: C

cards.term: 98% Noncoding REGULATES, 2% Coding makes Proteins
cards.definition:
🧬 GENOME ARCHITECTURE

📌 The phrase: The vast majority of the human genome doesn't code for proteins — but most of it isn't 'junk.' It controls when, where, and how much each gene is expressed.

◆ ~2% CODING — exons, the parts translated into proteins.
◆ ~98% NONCODING — regulatory elements (promoters, enhancers, silencers, insulators), non-coding RNAs (miRNAs, lncRNAs), repetitive elements, transposons, ancient viral integrations.
◆ Mutations in noncoding regions can have huge effects (e.g., enhancer changes alter limb morphology in vertebrates).

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Modern evolutionary biology is increasingly about REGULATORY change, not new genes. Most morphological evolution between humans and chimps is in regulatory regions, not coding sequence (King & Wilson 1975).

⚠ TRAP: 'Junk DNA' was the initial misnomer. ENCODE and similar projects show most noncoding DNA has biochemical activity, though debate continues over how much is functional vs neutral.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#6] Acetylation of histone tails generally:
  A. Triggers degradation of the protein the gene encodes.
  B. Causes alternative splicing of the resulting mRNA.
  C. Tightens chromatin and represses transcription.
  D. Loosens chromatin and promotes transcription.
→ Answer: D

[Final-C · MC#18] Which of the following is NOT considered part of the genome?
  A. Pseudogenes.
  B. Free amino acids in the cytoplasm.
  C. Mobile genetic elements.
  D. Protein-coding genes.
→ Answer: B

cards.term: TSTP: Transcription, Splicing, Translation, Post-translational
cards.definition:
🧬 FOUR LEVELS OF GENE EXPRESSION REGULATION

📌 The phrase: A gene's protein output can be controlled at any of 4 sequential steps. Mutations or signals at any level affect phenotype.

◆ TRANSCRIPTION — DNA → mRNA. Regulated by transcription factors binding promoters/enhancers. The most common control point.
◆ SPLICING — pre-mRNA → mature mRNA. Alternative splicing produces different protein isoforms from one gene. Hugely expands proteome.
◆ TRANSLATION — mRNA → protein. Regulated by ribosome availability, mRNA stability, miRNAs.
◆ POST-TRANSLATIONAL — protein modifications: phosphorylation, glycosylation, cleavage, folding, localization, degradation rate.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Evolution can act on any of these levels. Many adaptive differences between species are in regulatory mutations (transcription level), not coding sequence — making the same genome produce different phenotypes.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Lactase persistence in adults — regulatory mutation that keeps the LCT gene transcribed past childhood. Same coding sequence, different transcription regulation.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#6] Acetylation of histone tails generally:
  A. Triggers degradation of the protein the gene encodes.
  B. Causes alternative splicing of the resulting mRNA.
  C. Tightens chromatin and represses transcription.
  D. Loosens chromatin and promotes transcription.
→ Answer: D

[Final-D · MC#17] A microRNA binds to a complementary sequence in an mRNA and triggers its degradation. This is an example of:
  A. Pre-transcriptional regulation
  B. Post-transcriptional regulation
  C. Post-translational regulation
  D. Transcriptional regulation
→ Answer: B

cards.term: Alleles vs Genotypes: p is Allele freq, p² is Genotype freq
cards.definition:
⚖️ ALLELE FREQUENCIES vs GENOTYPE FREQUENCIES

📌 The phrase: Don't confuse the two. Alleles are units; genotypes are pairs.

◆ ALLELE FREQUENCY — fraction of all chromosome copies in the population that carry a given allele. p (for A) and q (for a). Sum = 1.
◆ GENOTYPE FREQUENCY — fraction of individuals with a given diploid combination. AA, Aa, aa.

📐 COMPUTING ALLELE FREQUENCY FROM GENOTYPES:
p = (2 × N_AA + N_Aa) / (2 × N_total)
Each AA contributes 2 A alleles; each Aa contributes 1; each aa contributes 0.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Hardy-Weinberg, breeder's equation, and most population-genetic equations work with ALLELE frequencies. Selection often acts on genotypes (phenotypes) but evolution = change in allele frequency.

🔬 EXAMPLE: 100 individuals: 36 AA, 48 Aa, 16 aa.
p = (72 + 48) / 200 = 0.6 ; q = 0.4
Under HWE you'd predict: AA=0.36, Aa=0.48, aa=0.16 — matches! No deviation here.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-B · MC#9] In a population of 200 diploid individuals, the genotype counts are 50 AA, 100 Aa, and 50 aa. What is the frequency of allele A?
  A. 0.75
  B. 0.50
  C. 0.40
  D. 0.25
→ Answer: B

[Final-C · MC#21] A population is started with 60% AA, 0% Aa, and 40% aa individuals. After one generation of random mating with all five HWE assumptions met, what are the genotype frequencies?
  A. 30% AA, 50% Aa, 20% aa
  B. 36% AA, 48% Aa, 16% aa
  C. 60% AA, 0% Aa, 40% aa (no change)
  D. 100% Aa (all heterozygous)
→ Answer: B

cards.term: χ² Test reveals deviation from HWE
cards.definition:
⚖️ DETECTING NON-HWE — WHY DEVIATIONS MATTER

📌 The phrase: When observed genotype counts ≠ HWE-expected counts, one of the 5 assumptions is being violated. Use a chi-squared (χ²) test.

◆ Compute expected counts under HWE: N × p², N × 2pq, N × q²
◆ Compare to observed using χ² = Σ (Obs−Exp)² / Exp
◆ Significant deviation → diagnose which mechanism (selection, drift, gene flow, mutation, non-random mating)

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: This is how population geneticists DETECT evolution from a snapshot of allele/genotype data. HWE serves as the null; deviation is the signal.

📐 COMMON DEVIATION PATTERNS:
→ Excess homozygotes → inbreeding, Wahlund effect, or selection against heterozygotes
→ Excess heterozygotes → outbreeding or heterozygote advantage (sickle-cell in malaria zones)
→ Allele frequencies shifting between generations → directional selection or migration

🔬 EXAMPLE: Sickle-cell in West Africa shows excess AS heterozygotes — diagnostic of heterozygote advantage maintained by malaria selection.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#23] Which of the following is NOT one of the five assumptions of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
  A. Random mating
  B. Infinite population size
  C. Equal allele frequencies
  D. No mutation
→ Answer: C

[Final-C · MC#21] A population is started with 60% AA, 0% Aa, and 40% aa individuals. After one generation of random mating with all five HWE assumptions met, what are the genotype frequencies?
  A. 30% AA, 50% Aa, 20% aa
  B. 36% AA, 48% Aa, 16% aa
  C. 60% AA, 0% Aa, 40% aa (no change)
  D. 100% Aa (all heterozygous)
→ Answer: B

cards.term: Selection without Heritability = NO Evolution
cards.definition:
📊 THE DISTINCTION THAT TRIPS PEOPLE UP

📌 The phrase: Selection acts every generation, but unless the trait is heritable (h² > 0), allele frequencies don't change between generations.

◆ Selection sorts the CURRENT generation by phenotype.
◆ Evolution requires the next generation to be DIFFERENT in allele frequency.
◆ The bridge between them is HERITABILITY.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Every cohort of organisms has selection acting on it (some die, some have more babies). But if the trait being selected on is purely environmental (not genetic), no evolution occurs. Common student trap.

🔬 EXAMPLE: A bodybuilder who lifts weights gains muscle (selection-like benefit). But the muscle isn't heritable — their kids start out with normal muscles. No evolution despite massive 'selection' on muscle.

⚠ TRAP: Many traits in plant breeding LOOK responsive to selection but are heavily environmental. Without measuring h², you can't predict response. R = h² × S — if h² ≈ 0, R ≈ 0.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#7] In which scenario does NATURAL SELECTION OCCUR but NO EVOLUTION result?
  A. A population shows heritable variation in beak depth, and large-beaked birds reproduce more during a drought.
  B. Two populations are separated by a mountain range and experience different selective pressures.
  C. A herd of cattle has variation in milk yield due entirely to feed differences (h² = 0)
  D. Bacteria exposed to antibiotics develop resistance through mutation.
→ Answer: C

[Final-B · MC#19] A trait has a large selection differential S but heritability h² = 0. What is the predicted response to selection R?
  A. Equal to S, since selection is strong.
  B. Negative — the population evolves the opposite way.
  C. Half of S, on average.
  D. R = 0, regardless of S.
→ Answer: D

cards.term: Adaptation: NOUN (the trait) AND VERB (the process)
cards.definition:
👁️ ADAPTATION — TWO MEANINGS, ONE WORD

📌 The phrase: 'Adaptation' refers to BOTH the evolved trait itself AND the process by which it evolved. Be clear which sense you mean.

◆ ADAPTATION (noun) — a trait shaped by past natural selection for its current function. Examples: the eye, hemoglobin, camouflage coloration.
◆ ADAPTATION (verb / process) — the historical process of natural selection that produced the trait. Driven by differential reproduction over generations.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Confusing the two leads to circular reasoning ('the eye is an adaptation because it helps you see, and it helps you see because it's an adaptation'). The proper test of an adaptation (noun) is the historical record + comparative methods, not present-day function.

📐 TEST FOR ADAPTATION:
→ The trait is HERITABLE
→ The trait IMPROVED reproductive success in the ancestors
→ The trait was selected SPECIFICALLY for that function (not a byproduct)
→ Comparative or experimental evidence supports its history

🔬 EXAMPLE: The vertebrate eye is an adaptation (both senses) — heritable, improves fitness, was selected for vision over millions of years.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#15] Whales have small, internal pelvic bones that don't articulate with the spine. What does this best illustrate?
  A. Pelvic bones formed by chance during whale development.
  B. Whales recently developed a pelvis through convergent evolution with mammals.
  C. Whales evolved from terrestrial ancestors that had functional pelvic skeletons
  D. These bones support the whale's swimming musculature in a major way.
→ Answer: C

[Final-A · MC#28] Which of the following best illustrates coevolution (rather than mere coexistence or convergence)?
  A. Two species of cactus in the same desert evolving similar water-storage tissue.
  B. Two unrelated frogs in different continents evolving the same toxic compound.
  C. Different bird species nesting in the same forest without interacting.
  D. A predator and its prey both evolving faster running speeds in response to one another.
→ Answer: D

cards.term: Tinkered, Not Engineered
cards.definition:
👁️ IMPERFECT ADAPTATION — EVOLUTION IS A TINKERER

📌 The phrase: Evolution doesn't redesign from scratch — it modifies what's already there. The result is functional but often jury-rigged.

◆ EVOLUTION CAN'T:
  → start over
  → look ahead
  → choose the best design — only the best NEXT step from current state

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Many features that seem 'designed' badly become understandable as constrained evolution from ancestors:

📐 CLASSIC EXAMPLES OF IMPERFECT ADAPTATION:
→ RECURRENT LARYNGEAL NERVE — runs from brain DOWN past the heart and BACK up to the larynx. In giraffes it makes a 4 m detour. Vestige of fish ancestry where the path was direct.
→ HUMAN BLIND SPOT — vertebrate retina is 'inside-out' (photoreceptors face away from light, blood vessels and nerves on TOP of the retina). Octopus eye has it right.
→ APPENDIX — vestigial structure with minor immune function but mostly a relic of cecum.
→ WISDOM TEETH — too many teeth for modern jaw size.
→ BIRTH DIFFICULTIES — bipedal pelvis is too narrow for big-brained babies.

🔬 EXAMPLE: François Jacob (1977 essay 'Evolution and Tinkering') — evolution has been compared to a tinkerer who 'works without an idea of what he is going to make.' Captures it perfectly.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#15] Whales have small, internal pelvic bones that don't articulate with the spine. What does this best illustrate?
  A. Pelvic bones formed by chance during whale development.
  B. Whales recently developed a pelvis through convergent evolution with mammals.
  C. Whales evolved from terrestrial ancestors that had functional pelvic skeletons
  D. These bones support the whale's swimming musculature in a major way.
→ Answer: C

[Final-C · MC#29] The vertebrate eye and the cephalopod eye are both camera-type eyes with lens, retina, and pupil. They are best described as:
  A. An example of horizontal gene transfer.
  B. Convergent (analogous) structures
  C. Vestigial structures — both eyes are functional,
  D. Homologous structures inherited from a common eyed ancestor.
→ Answer: B

cards.term: Red Queen Runs in Place
cards.definition:
🦋 ANTAGONISTIC COEVOLUTIONARY ARMS RACE

📌 The phrase: From Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass — 'It takes all the running you can do, to keep in the same place.' Van Valen (1973) used this to describe coevolution where each side just runs to keep up with the other.

◆ Predator improves hunting → prey evolve better defenses → predator must adapt → and so on
◆ Host immune system evolves → parasite evolves evasion → host evolves new immunity
◆ NEITHER side gets ahead long term — both keep evolving without net 'progress'

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Explains:
→ Why parasites evolve so fast (constant immune pressure)
→ Why immune systems are so complex (constant parasite pressure)
→ One reason sex evolved (recombination keeps host genomes a moving target)
→ Why arms races can drive extreme escalation (newt toxin/garter snake resistance)

🔬 EXAMPLE: Garter snakes (Thamnophis sirtalis) eat newts (Taricha) that contain TTX, one of the most lethal toxins known. Some snake populations are TTX-resistant; their newts have evolved more TTX. Co-escalating arms race.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#19] The Red Queen hypothesis proposes that sexual reproduction is favored because:
  A. Predators preferentially attack asexual species.
  B. Sex makes reproduction faster than asexual processes.
  C. Sexual reproduction reduces parental investment in each offspring.
  D. Hosts must constantly evolve to keep up with rapidly evolving parasites
→ Answer: D

[Final-D · MC#12] Rough-skinned newts (Taricha) produce tetrodotoxin (TTX); garter snakes (Thamnophis) eat them. In some regions, snakes are highly TTX-resistant; in others, they have little resistance. What does this geographic variation suggest?
  A. There is a coevolutionary geographic mosaic: 'hotspots' of intense reciprocal selection alternate with 'coldspots' of weak interaction.
  B. Snake populations migrate between regions, equalizing resistance over time.
  C. TTX evolved before snakes evolved resistance, and resistance is still spreading.
  D. Coevolution is not actually occurring — the trait is just genetically variable.
→ Answer: A

cards.term: Figs Need Wasps, Wasps Need Figs
cards.definition:
🦋 OBLIGATE MUTUALISTIC COEVOLUTION

📌 The phrase: Each fig species is pollinated by ONE specific fig wasp species; the wasp lays eggs only inside that fig. Total interdependence.

◆ Female wasp enters fig (loses wings, can't leave); pollinates flowers and lays eggs.
◆ Eggs hatch into larvae; mate inside fig; new females emerge with pollen from this fig and fly to find another fig species mate.
◆ NEITHER species can reproduce without the other.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Mutualistic coevolution can produce stable, intricate dependencies — but also fragile ones. Lose one partner and the other goes extinct. Such tight coevolution is most common in:
→ Pollination (figs/wasps, yucca/yucca moth)
→ Mycorrhizal fungi/plant roots
→ Lichens (fungus + alga/cyanobacterium)
→ Mitochondria/eukaryotic cells (ancient endosymbiosis)

🔬 EXAMPLE: ~750 fig species, each with a specific wasp pollinator. The fig's complex morphology only makes sense in light of the wasp's life cycle inside it.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#28] Which of the following best illustrates coevolution (rather than mere coexistence or convergence)?
  A. Two species of cactus in the same desert evolving similar water-storage tissue.
  B. Two unrelated frogs in different continents evolving the same toxic compound.
  C. Different bird species nesting in the same forest without interacting.
  D. A predator and its prey both evolving faster running speeds in response to one another.
→ Answer: D

[Final-D · MC#12] Rough-skinned newts (Taricha) produce tetrodotoxin (TTX); garter snakes (Thamnophis) eat them. In some regions, snakes are highly TTX-resistant; in others, they have little resistance. What does this geographic variation suggest?
  A. There is a coevolutionary geographic mosaic: 'hotspots' of intense reciprocal selection alternate with 'coldspots' of weak interaction.
  B. Snake populations migrate between regions, equalizing resistance over time.
  C. TTX evolved before snakes evolved resistance, and resistance is still spreading.
  D. Coevolution is not actually occurring — the trait is just genetically variable.
→ Answer: A

cards.term: Sex's 2-Fold Cost: 50% Genes Lost, 100% Hassle
cards.definition:
⚥ THE COST OF SEX (Maynard Smith 1971)

📌 The phrase: An asexual female passes 100% of her genes to each daughter. A sexual female passes only 50% (the other half comes from the male). Asexual reproduction should reproductively double-out sex — yet most eukaryotes are sexual.

◆ 50% GENES LOST — the 'twofold cost of males' (or 'cost of meiosis'). Each offspring inherits half your genes; the other half comes from someone else.
◆ 100% HASSLE — finding a mate takes time; courtship is risky; STDs; sexual conflict; predation while mating.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: This is the puzzle that sexual-selection and Red-Queen theories try to solve. Sex is everywhere despite costing twofold per generation — there must be a SUBSTANTIAL benefit.

📐 BENEFITS THAT OUTWEIGH THE COST:
→ Recombination breaks up linked deleterious mutations (Muller's Ratchet)
→ New genotypes outpace coevolving parasites (Red Queen)
→ Tangled Bank: genotypic variety lets siblings exploit different niches
→ Repair of DNA damage during meiosis

⚠ TRAP: Bdelloid rotifers are 80+ MY asexual — but apparently survive via massive horizontal gene transfer + extreme stress tolerance. They cheat the cost.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#25] What is the 'twofold cost of sex' (Maynard Smith)?
  A. Sexual reproduction produces twice as much genetic variation as asexual.
  B. Sexual species have twice the mutation rate of asexual species.
  C. A sexual female passes on only half as many of her genes per offspring (compared to an asexual female who would transmit all her genes).
  D. Sexual reproduction takes twice as long as asexual reproduction.
→ Answer: C

[Final-D · MC#11] Muller's ratchet describes:
  A. Loss of beneficial alleles by drift in small sexual populations.
  B. The clicking sound of bacterial flagella.
  C. A directional ratchet of beneficial mutations in sexual populations.
  D. Irreversible accumulation of deleterious mutations in asexual populations
→ Answer: D

cards.term: Sexual Selection = Darwin's SECOND Mechanism
cards.definition:
⚥ SEXUAL SELECTION — DISTINCT FROM NATURAL SELECTION

📌 The phrase: Darwin (1871, Descent of Man) introduced sexual selection as a SEPARATE mechanism — selection on traits that improve mating success even at the cost of survival.

◆ NATURAL SELECTION — selects for survival traits (camouflage, food-finding, disease resistance)
◆ SEXUAL SELECTION — selects for mating-success traits (ornament, song, combat)
◆ The two can OPPOSE each other: peacock tail is bad for survival but good for mating

📐 TWO MODES OF SEXUAL SELECTION:
→ INTRASEXUAL — same-sex competition (male-male combat: antlers, horns, body size)
→ INTERSEXUAL — opposite-sex choice (typically female choice: ornaments, song, courtship)

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Many of biology's most spectacular traits (peacock tail, elk antlers, bird-of-paradise displays) make NO sense under survival selection alone. They only make sense if mating success outweighs survival cost.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Long tails in widowbirds — Andersson (1982) experimentally LENGTHENED some males' tails and SHORTENED others. Long-tail males got more mates despite the survival cost. Direct evidence for sexual selection by female choice.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#30] Male elk grow large antlers used in physical combat with rival males during the breeding season. This is primarily an example of:
  A. Sexual conflict — sexual conflict is between
  B. Intrasexual selection (same-sex competition).
  C. Intersexual selection (mate choice).
  D. Sexual cooperation — combat is competitive, not
→ Answer: B

[Final-C · MC#22] Female peahens prefer males with larger, more iridescent tails. Male peacock tails reduce survival (visible to predators, costly to grow). The persistence of the tail despite its survival cost is best explained by:
  A. Intersexual selection (mate choice) outweighing the survival cost.
  B. Group selection for showy populations — group selection isn't needed
  C. Intrasexual selection — males physically fight with their tails.
  D. Sexual conflict — females can't tell males with tails apart from males without.
→ Answer: A

cards.term: Direct Benefits (resources) vs Indirect Benefits (good genes)
cards.definition:
⚥ WHY DO FEMALES CHOOSE? — TWO BENEFIT TYPES

📌 The phrase: When a female chooses a mate, she may gain DIRECT benefits (something material she gets right now) or INDIRECT benefits (better genes for her offspring).

◆ DIRECT BENEFITS — tangible resources received from the male:
  → Nuptial gifts (food)
  → Parental care for the offspring
  → Quality territory or nest site
  → Protection from harassment by other males

◆ INDIRECT BENEFITS — better genes for offspring (no direct payoff to female herself):
  → 'Good genes' — male displays signal heritable quality (Hamilton-Zuk parasite resistance, Zahavi handicap)
  → 'Sexy sons' — sons inherit attractive traits, get more mates (Fisher runaway)

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Predicts WHICH SEX should be choosier. If males offer big direct benefits (parental care), females become VERY choosy. If males offer only sperm, females can be less choosy or rely on indirect benefits.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Hangingflies — males catch prey for 'nuptial gifts' before mating. Females reject males with small gifts. Direct benefit selection. Bird-of-paradise — males offer NO direct benefits; female choice based purely on display = indirect benefit selection.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-C · MC#22] Female peahens prefer males with larger, more iridescent tails. Male peacock tails reduce survival (visible to predators, costly to grow). The persistence of the tail despite its survival cost is best explained by:
  A. Intersexual selection (mate choice) outweighing the survival cost.
  B. Group selection for showy populations — group selection isn't needed
  C. Intrasexual selection — males physically fight with their tails.
  D. Sexual conflict — females can't tell males with tails apart from males without.
→ Answer: A

[Final-B · MC#22] Fisherian runaway sexual selection refers to:
  A. Mutation pressure generating new ornament traits.
  B. A positive-feedback process where female preference for a male trait and the trait itself co-amplify over generations
  C. Predators learning to avoid mating displays of unpalatable species.
  D. Loss of all sexual ornaments due to high predation.
→ Answer: B

cards.term: Sperm Compete, Females Cryptic-Choose
cards.definition:
⚥ POST-MATING SEXUAL CONFLICT

📌 The phrase: Sexual selection doesn't end at mating. Inside the female reproductive tract, sperm from different males compete, and females can 'cryptically' favor some sperm over others.

◆ SPERM COMPETITION — when a female mates with multiple males, their sperm physically compete for fertilization. Larger ejaculates, faster swimmers, sperm plugs, sperm-displacing genitalia.
◆ CRYPTIC FEMALE CHOICE — female reproductive tract differentially admits, stores, or uses sperm from different males. Choice happens AFTER mating, invisible to outside observers.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Sexual selection extends beyond visible courtship. Many species' genitalia are bizarre because they're shaped by sperm-competition + cryptic-choice arms races. Drives surprisingly fast evolution of reproductive anatomy.

🔬 EXAMPLE:
→ Damselfly males have 'penis scoops' that remove a previous male's sperm before adding their own.
→ Female ducks have spiral-shaped reproductive tracts that can divert sperm from forced copulations.
→ Honeybee males' genitalia explode and break off inside the queen, blocking subsequent males (mating plug).

⚠ TRAP: Don't confuse with kin selection or cooperative breeding — this is post-mating sexual selection, an extension of mate-choice into the body.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-B · MC#10] Species in which females mate with multiple males within a single breeding cycle tend to evolve relatively LARGE TESTES compared to species with strictly monogamous mating. The most likely explanation is:
  A. Sperm competition — males who produce more sperm have higher chances of fertilizing ova when ejaculate from rival males is also present.
  B. Larger testes are required for hormone signaling.
  C. Larger testes evolved randomly via drift — the pattern is too strong and consistent across
  D. Larger testes in polyandrous species support larger overall body size.
→ Answer: A

[Final-C · MC#15] In Drosophila, male seminal fluid contains compounds that increase female short-term egg-laying but reduce female lifespan. From a sexual-conflict perspective:
  A. This is mutualism — both sexes benefit equally.
  B. Females have evolved zero counter-adaptations to these compounds.
  C. The compounds randomly evolved with no selective basis.
  D. Male and female evolutionary interests diverge: males benefit from immediate fertilization even at long-term cost to females.
→ Answer: D

cards.term: Group Selection Mostly REJECTED — Free-Riders Win
cards.definition:
🤝 INDIVIDUAL vs GROUP SELECTION

📌 The phrase: 'For the good of the species' explanations are mostly WRONG. Selection acts on individuals (or genes), not groups. Group selection arguments fall to the free-rider problem.

◆ FREE-RIDER PROBLEM — within any cooperating group, a 'cheater' who takes the benefits without paying the cost has higher individual fitness. Cheaters spread, cooperation collapses.
◆ Williams (1966, Adaptation and Natural Selection) — devastating critique. 'Adaptations of organisms exist for the good of the organism, not the species.'
◆ Group selection CAN work in narrow conditions (very small groups, strong group founding events, low migration), but is generally weaker than individual-level selection.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Tons of natural-history claims ('animals limit their breeding for the good of the population,' 'lemmings sacrifice themselves for the species') are WRONG. Real cooperation is explained by KIN SELECTION (Hamilton's rule rB > C), reciprocity, or byproduct mutualism — not group selection.

📐 ALTERNATIVES TO GROUP SELECTION:
→ Kin selection (rB > C) — explains alarm calls, sterile castes, helpers-at-the-nest
→ Reciprocity (tit-for-tat) — explains non-kin cooperation
→ Multilevel selection — modern statistical framework that includes group-level effects

⚠ TRAP: Wynne-Edwards's group-selection arguments (1962) for population regulation were the textbook example of WRONG — animals don't restrict reproduction for population good.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#14] Why is naïve group selection — the idea that traits evolve 'for the good of the species' — generally rejected in modern evolutionary biology?
  A. Group benefits are physically impossible.
  B. Species don't actually exist as discrete entities.
  C. A 'cheater' that exploits cooperation has higher individual fitness than cooperators
  D. Group selection only works when the cosmos approves.
→ Answer: C

[Final-A · MC#25] Worker honey bees forgo reproduction and help raise their queen's offspring. From an inclusive-fitness perspective, this makes sense because:
  A. Workers are sterile and incapable of reproduction.
  B. Workers gain inclusive fitness by helping raise sisters (in haplodiploid systems
  C. Group selection at the colony level overrides individual fitness.
  D. Workers are forced into helping by the queen and have no choice.
→ Answer: B

cards.term: Reading Trees: Rotations Don't Matter, Only Branching
cards.definition:
🌳 HOW TO READ A PHYLOGENETIC TREE

📌 The phrase: A phylogeny tells you NESTING (who shares an ancestor with whom), NOT order along the tips. Rotating any branch around its node changes nothing about relationships.

◆ TIPS — extant or sampled taxa.
◆ NODES — common ancestors (last shared ancestor of the descendant lineages).
◆ BRANCHES — lineages through time.
◆ SISTER GROUPS — two clades that share a most recent common ancestor with each other.
◆ MONOPHYLETIC GROUP (clade) — a node + ALL its descendants.

📐 KEY READING RULES:
→ Trees can be ROTATED at any node without changing the topology. (Human and chimp can be drawn on either side.)
→ Distance along the tip axis does NOT mean evolutionary distance unless the tree is scaled.
→ Branch length CAN encode time or genetic change — depends on the tree type.
→ The order of tips along the bottom is COSMETIC.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Most students misread trees as a 'progression' from primitive to advanced. Trees are HISTORICAL networks of common ancestry — no species is 'higher' than another; all extant tips have equal time since their common ancestor.

🔬 EXAMPLE: A tree showing fish (left) → frog → mouse → human (right) does NOT mean human is 'highest.' Humans and mice diverged from a shared ancestor; both are tips of equal age since that split. Drawing the tips in any other order tells the same story.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#24] On a phylogenetic tree, two taxa are 'more closely related' to each other than to a third when:
  A. Their lineages have evolved at similar rates.
  B. Their branches end closer together horizontally on the page.
  C. They share a more recent common ancestor (a more shallow node) than either does with the third.
  D. They share more morphological similarities overall.
→ Answer: C

[Final-B · MC#21] The traditional group 'Reptilia' (turtles, lizards, snakes, crocodiles) excludes birds. Birds, however, are descended from theropod dinosaurs, nested within Reptilia by descent. What kind of group is traditional 'Reptilia'?
  A. Diphyletic — has exactly two ancestral origins.
  B. Polyphyletic — members lack an immediate common ancestor.
  C. Paraphyletic — includes a common ancestor and SOME but not all of its descendants.
  D. Monophyletic — it's a clade — a clade includes ALL descendants
→ Answer: C

cards.term: 3 Hybrid Zone Models: Tension, Mosaic, Bounded Superiority
cards.definition:
🐦 HYBRID ZONES — WHERE SPECIES MEET

📌 The phrase: When two diverged species come into contact, a hybrid zone may form. Three models explain how it stays stable.

◆ TENSION ZONE — hybrids are LESS fit than either parent (postzygotic isolation). Zone is maintained by balance between gene flow into the zone and selection against hybrids inside it. Width set by dispersal × selection.
◆ MOSAIC — environment is patchy; species 1 fits one habitat type, species 2 fits another, hybrids might fit intermediate or transition zones. Hybrid frequency varies in space.
◆ BOUNDED SUPERIORITY — hybrids are fitter than EITHER parent in a narrow zone of intermediate environment, but parents do better outside it. Hybrid 'fitness island' surrounded by parental zones.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Hybrid zones are natural laboratories for studying:
→ How reproductive isolation evolves
→ Strength and timing of postzygotic barriers
→ Whether reinforcement is happening (do prezygotic barriers strengthen?)
→ Genetic architecture of species differences

🔬 EXAMPLE:
→ Tension zone: fire-bellied + yellow-bellied toads in Europe (Bombina) — narrow zone, hybrids unfit.
→ Mosaic: oak species in eastern US (Quercus) — local hybridization in patches.
→ Bounded superiority: some Iris hybrids in Louisiana — hybrid swarms in specific microhabitats.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#29] A hybrid zone exists where two species' ranges overlap and they interbreed, producing low-fitness hybrids. Does the existence of this hybrid zone disprove the species' status under the BSC?
  A. Cannot be determined without additional evidence.
  B. Yes — only completely non-interbreeding populations are species.
  C. No — if hybrids have reduced fitness, gene flow remains limited
  D. Yes — any interbreeding means they are the same species.
→ Answer: C

[Final-B · MC#16] Horses and donkeys mate and produce viable offspring (mules), but mules are sterile. This is best classified as:
  A. Prezygotic isolation — behavioral.
  B. Postzygotic isolation — hybrid sterility.
  C. Postzygotic isolation — hybrid inviability.
  D. Prezygotic isolation — gametic.
→ Answer: B

cards.term: Biogeography: Where Life Lives + WHY
cards.definition:
🗺️ WHAT BIOGEOGRAPHY STUDIES

📌 The phrase: Biogeography asks two questions about every species: Where does it live? Why THERE and not elsewhere?

◆ DESCRIPTIVE — mapping current distributions and biogeographic regions (Wallace's 6 zoogeographic regions, Holdridge life zones)
◆ HISTORICAL — explaining current distributions through past events (continental drift, climate, dispersal, vicariance, mass extinctions)
◆ ECOLOGICAL — explaining distributions through current environmental tolerances (climate, soil, biotic interactions)

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Biogeography was Darwin's strongest evidence for evolution. Why do oceanic islands have endemic species closely related to mainland? Why does Australia have marsupials but not native placental mammals? These patterns make NO sense under separate creation, perfect sense under descent with modification + geography.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Galápagos finches resemble mainland Ecuadorean finches (closest source area), not finches from any other continent. This is geography-driven phylogeny — the islands were colonized from the nearest mainland, then radiated.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#9] Biogeography is best defined as the study of:
  A. The distribution of species and ecosystems in geographic space and through geological time.
  B. Genetic differences within a single population.
  C. How organisms differ chemically.
  D. Climate change effects on individual organisms.
→ Answer: A

[Final-C · MC#30] The Wallace Line is:
  A. A line on a phylogenetic tree separating chordates from arthropods.
  B. A faunal boundary in the Indonesian archipelago that separates Asian and Australasian biotas
  C. A genetic marker used to date the human-chimpanzee split.
  D. The boundary of Wallace's voyage on the HMS Beagle.
→ Answer: B

cards.term: Survivors RADIATE After Mass Extinctions
cards.definition:
🦖 ADAPTIVE RADIATION FOLLOWS EXTINCTION

📌 The phrase: When a mass extinction empties ecological niches, surviving lineages diversify rapidly into the vacated roles. Mass extinctions are RESET BUTTONS.

◆ Pre-extinction: niches filled by dominant groups (e.g., dinosaurs)
◆ Mass extinction: dominants wiped out
◆ Post-extinction: small/peripheral lineages with the right traits diversify into open niches
→ Cretaceous mammals were small, marginal, mostly nocturnal
→ K-Pg killed the dinosaurs (66 MYA)
→ Cenozoic mammals exploded into all sizes/lifestyles within 10-15 MY

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Modern biodiversity is shaped as much by which lineages SURVIVED extinctions as by which ones evolved well during quiet times. The 'rules of survival' during mass extinctions (broad geographic range, ecological generalism, small body size) often differ from rules of success during normal times.

🔬 EXAMPLE:
→ K-Pg extinction → mammal radiation (and bird radiation among avian dinosaurs)
→ Permian extinction → dinosaurs dominated the next era
→ End-Devonian → tetrapods radiated onto land
→ Current 6th extinction (anthropogenic) → it's too early to know who will radiate next, but generalists (rats, raccoons, cockroaches) are favored.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-B · MC#26] Why did mammals undergo a major adaptive radiation after the K-Pg extinction?
  A. Mammals appeared for the first time after the K-Pg.
  B. Mammals were not affected by the asteroid impact.
  C. Mammals had higher mutation rates after the extinction.
  D. Mammals had been small and ecologically restricted
→ Answer: D

[Final-D · MC#22] Which condition most strongly favors adaptive radiation?
  A. Genetic drift in a single population.
  B. Open ecological space (e.g.
  C. High predation pressure.
  D. A stable, fully occupied ecosystem.
→ Answer: B

cards.term: Bottleneck → Drift → Inbreeding Depression
cards.definition:
🌡️ ANTHROPOGENIC EVOLUTION — POPULATION FRAGMENTATION

📌 The phrase: Habitat destruction shrinks populations. Small populations lose genetic diversity to drift, then suffer inbreeding depression.

◆ BOTTLENECK — population size crashes (often human-caused: hunting, habitat loss). Most alleles lost; only the survivors' genomes remain. New population is genetically depleted.
◆ DRIFT — small N → strong drift → loss of further alleles, fixation of others by chance.
◆ INBREEDING DEPRESSION — small isolated populations have to mate among relatives. Recessive deleterious alleles get exposed in homozygotes. Reduced fitness.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: This is the central conservation-genetic problem. Once populations drop below a critical size (~50-500 effective N), genetic erosion accelerates and recovery is hard even if habitat is restored.

🔬 EXAMPLE:
→ CHEETAHS — went through severe bottleneck ~10,000 years ago. All cheetahs alive today are ≈ as related as full siblings. Sperm abnormality, susceptibility to disease.
→ FLORIDA PANTHERS — by 1990s, ~30 individuals remained, severely inbred (heart defects, undescended testicles, kinked tails). Genetic rescue by introducing 8 Texas pumas in 1995 RESTORED fitness within a generation.
→ NORTHERN ELEPHANT SEAL — bottleneck of ~20 in 1890s. Today ~200,000 but with extremely low genetic diversity.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-B · MC#2] Florida panthers (a remnant subpopulation of cougars) suffered severe inbreeding depression. Conservation managers introduced cougars from Texas. The Florida population's fitness improved significantly. This intervention is called:
  A. Convergent evolution.
  B. Sympatric speciation.
  C. Captive breeding.
  D. Genetic rescue.
→ Answer: D

[Final-A · MC#13] Inbreeding depression in a small population arises because:
  A. Inbreeding increases homozygosity
  B. Inbreeding only affects sexually selected traits.
  C. Inbreeding causes new mutations.
  D. Inbreeding directly reduces population size.
→ Answer: A

cards.term: Climate Change = Directional Selection on Phenology
cards.definition:
🌡️ ANTHROPOGENIC EVOLUTION — CLIMATE CHANGE

📌 The phrase: Climate change is acting as a directional selective force on the TIMING of biological events (phenology) — flowering, breeding, migration, leaf-out.

◆ Warmer springs → earlier optimal time for many activities
◆ Selection favors individuals that can advance their phenology
◆ Some species respond (heritable shift); some don't (extinction risk)

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: We're watching evolution happen in real time on continental scales. Three possible outcomes for any species facing climate change:
→ ADAPT (evolve fast enough) — requires heritable variation in relevant traits
→ MIGRATE (range shift) — requires connected habitat
→ DIE (local extinction) — most likely if neither of the above is possible

🔬 EXAMPLE:
→ EUROPEAN BLACKCAPS — wintering migrations have shifted from Spain to UK over decades, driven by warmer winters AND human bird-feeders. Heritable change in migratory direction.
→ PIED FLYCATCHERS — caterpillar peak shifts earlier with warming, but flycatcher arrival timing isn't shifting fast enough → declining populations.
→ MOUNTAIN PINE BEETLES — range expansion in BC due to warmer winters that no longer kill larvae. Massive ecological consequence.

⚠ TRAP: 'Adapt or migrate' isn't a guarantee — many species lack genetic variation, suitable habitat, or time. Climate change is producing the 6th mass extinction.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#24] Many bird species are now breeding earlier in spring than they did 50 years ago. This represents:
  A. Hybridization between bird species.
  B. A phenological shift
  C. A purely behavioral choice with no evolutionary basis.
  D. A speciation event — earlier breeding within
→ Answer: B

[Final-C · MC#6] Caterpillars now emerge earlier in spring due to warming. The bird species that depends on those caterpillars for chick food now arrives at the breeding grounds AFTER the caterpillar peak. This is called:
  A. Convergent evolution.
  B. Inclusive fitness.
  C. Phenological mismatch.
  D. Coevolution.
→ Answer: C

cards.term: Australopiths Walked First, Brains Came Later
cards.definition:
🧠 AUSTRALOPITHECINES — BIPEDAL APES

📌 The phrase: Australopithecines (4-2 MYA) were the first clearly bipedal hominins, but with chimp-sized brains. Sets up the 'mosaic evolution' point.

◆ FOOT/PELVIS ANATOMY — fully adapted to bipedalism by 3.5 MYA at the latest.
◆ BRAIN SIZE — Australopithecus brains ~400-500 cc (chimp range). Human brains 1300-1400 cc.
◆ TOOL USE — limited evidence; some Oldowan-like tools associated with later Australopiths.

📐 KEY SPECIES:
→ A. anamensis (4.2-3.9 MYA, Kenya)
