→ A. afarensis ('Lucy,' 3.9-2.9 MYA, East Africa)
→ A. africanus (3-2 MYA, South Africa)
→ Paranthropus robustus/boisei (2.7-1 MYA) — 'robust' lineage with massive jaws for tough vegetation; went extinct.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Australopithecines prove BIPEDALISM came first in human evolution; brain enlargement came in genus Homo (~2 MYA onward). Refutes any 'big brain made us walk' scenario.

📖 STORY: 1924 — the Taung Child (A. africanus) was the first African australopithecine found by Raymond Dart. Skeptically received in Europe (which expected human ancestors in Asia/Europe, not Africa). Vindicated only after the 1950s.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Laetoli footprints (3.6 MYA, Tanzania) — preserved bipedal footprints from a small group of A. afarensis walking through fresh volcanic ash. Direct evidence of fully modern bipedal gait — long before tools or large brains.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#21] 'Lucy' is a famous specimen of which species?
  A. Australopithecus afarensis
  B. Sahelanthropus tchadensis
  C. Homo neanderthalensis
  D. Homo erectus
→ Answer: A

[Final-B · MC#29] Bipedal locomotion in the hominin lineage began approximately:
  A. 6–7 million years ago
  B. 200,000 years ago
  C. 100 million years ago
  D. 1 million years ago
→ Answer: A

cards.term: Why We're Sick: Evolution Didn't Optimize for Modernity
cards.definition:
💊 WHAT EVOLUTIONARY MEDICINE IS

📌 The phrase: Evolutionary medicine asks WHY our bodies are vulnerable to disease — explanations that go beyond proximate mechanisms (how it goes wrong) to ULTIMATE causes (why selection didn't fix it).

📐 6 PROXIMATE/ULTIMATE QUESTIONS (Nesse & Williams):
1. Mismatch — modern environment differs from ancestral one (diet, sedentary lifestyle)
2. Coevolution with pathogens — Red Queen, parasites evolve faster than we do
3. Constraints — physics and history limit what selection could optimize
4. Trade-offs — antagonistic pleiotropy, every benefit has a cost
5. Reproduction over health — selection cares about offspring count, not lifespan
6. Defenses (vs disease) — fever, pain, anxiety are EVOLVED responses, not always disease

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Reframes medicine. Suppressing fever or anxiety may be wrong if these are adaptive responses. Targeting evolved trade-offs may yield better treatments. Public health interventions (clean water, vaccinations) work in part by changing the SELECTION ENVIRONMENT for pathogens.

🔬 EXAMPLE: Iron-withholding by the body during infection — long misunderstood as 'anemia of inflammation.' Actually an evolved DEFENSE: bacteria need iron, hiding it from them slows infection. Iron supplementation during active infection can WORSEN outcomes.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#10] Type 2 diabetes is rare in traditional hunter-gatherer populations and prevalent in industrialized populations. Which evolutionary explanation best fits?
  A. Mismatch — traits adaptive in ancestral environments (efficient fat storage
  B. Industrialized populations have weaker immune systems.
  C. Hunter-gatherers have higher mutation rates that prevent diabetes.
  D. Hunter-gatherers do not have the genes for diabetes.
→ Answer: A

[Final-C · MC#12] Evolutionary medicine differs from conventional medicine primarily by:
  A. Asking WHY (in evolutionary terms) bodies are vulnerable to disease
  B. Using evolutionary concepts to oppose vaccination and antibiotics.
  C. Focusing only on infectious disease — evolutionary medicine spans infectious disease,
  D. Replacing modern medical practice with paleolithic remedies.
→ Answer: A

cards.term: Host-Pathogen Red Queen: Both Run in Place
cards.definition:
💊 HOST-PATHOGEN COEVOLUTION

📌 The phrase: Host immune systems and pathogens are locked in a perpetual coevolutionary arms race. Neither side ever 'wins' — both keep evolving forever.

◆ Host evolves immune defenses (MHC diversity, antibody repertoire)
◆ Pathogen evolves evasion (antigenic variation, immune suppression)
◆ Host evolves new countermeasures
◆ Cycle continues — neither side gets ahead long term

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: Explains:
→ Why we still get sick despite a sophisticated immune system
→ Why MHC genes are the most polymorphic in the human genome (negative frequency-dependent selection — rare immunotypes win)
→ Why pathogen genome evolution is so fast (constant immune pressure)
→ Why annual flu vaccines need updating (virus evolves antigens annually)
→ One major hypothesis for the maintenance of sex itself

🔬 EXAMPLE:
→ INFLUENZA — antigenic drift (mutations in HA/NA proteins) + antigenic shift (reassortment between strains) keeps the virus ahead of human immunity. Vaccines must update yearly.
→ HIV — extreme intra-host evolution; quasispecies cloud allows escape from immune responses, drugs.
→ MALARIA — Plasmodium has var genes coding for variant surface antigens; can switch them during a single infection to evade host immunity.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-D · MC#27] MHC genes show extreme polymorphism — some loci have >100 alleles in human populations. The most likely cause is:
  A. Gene conversion homogenizing the locus.
  B. Negative frequency-dependent (balancing) selection from coevolving pathogens
  C. Random mutation alone, with no selection.
  D. Genetic drift in large populations.
→ Answer: B

[Final-A · MC#19] The Red Queen hypothesis proposes that sexual reproduction is favored because:
  A. Predators preferentially attack asexual species.
  B. Sex makes reproduction faster than asexual processes.
  C. Sexual reproduction reduces parental investment in each offspring.
  D. Hosts must constantly evolve to keep up with rapidly evolving parasites
→ Answer: D

cards.term: Vaccines Target CONSERVED Epitopes
cards.definition:
💊 VACCINE DESIGN UNDER PATHOGEN EVOLUTION

📌 The phrase: Effective vaccines target parts of pathogens that CAN'T evolve much without breaking the pathogen. Variable parts are escape hatches.

◆ CONSERVED EPITOPES — under purifying selection, mutations are removed because they break critical function. Targeting them works long-term.
◆ VARIABLE EPITOPES — under positive (escape) selection. Pathogen can mutate around immune pressure. Vaccines targeting these become obsolete fast.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: This evolutionary logic guides vaccine design:
→ Universal flu vaccine attempts target the conserved HA stalk, not the variable HA head
→ HIV vaccines try to target conserved Env regions, but HIV's escape capacity is enormous
→ COVID-19 mRNA vaccines targeted spike (somewhat conserved) — boosters needed as new variants emerged with spike mutations

📐 OTHER EVOLUTIONARILY-INFORMED INTERVENTIONS:
→ Combination antibiotic therapy (similar idea to antiretroviral cocktails for HIV) — pathogen needs to mutate at multiple sites simultaneously to escape
→ Dosing schedules to minimize selection for resistance
→ Vaccinating before pathogen exposure (prevents intra-host evolution under partial immunity)

⚠ TRAP: 'Leaky' vaccines (don't fully prevent infection or transmission) can create selection for MORE virulent strains in some pathogens (Marek's disease in chickens) — counterintuitive evolutionary outcome.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-C · MC#1] HIV is treated with COMBINATION antiretroviral therapy (multiple drugs simultaneously) rather than a single drug. What is the evolutionary rationale?
  A. Multiple drugs cure HIV completely.
  B. Multiple drugs improve patient compliance.
  C. Resistance to multiple drugs simultaneously
  D. Multiple drugs work in different organs.
→ Answer: C

[Final-B · MC#23] Influenza virus rapidly evolves resistance to antiviral drugs. Which statement best captures the role of mutation in this process?
  A. Antiviral exposure causes the virus to mutate toward resistance.
  B. The drug induces directed mutations only in the genes that confer resistance.
  C. Mutations conferring resistance arise by chance independently of drug presence
  D. Resistance is acquired during the host's lifetime and passed to offspring viruses through epigenetic inheritance.
→ Answer: C

cards.term: All Life Shares ONE LUCA (Last Universal Common Ancestor)
cards.definition:
🌳 SYNTHESIS: THE TREE OF LIFE

📌 The phrase: Every organism alive today, from bacteria to whales, descends from ONE common ancestor that lived ~3.8 BYA. Universal common ancestry is the deepest pattern in biology.

📐 EVIDENCE FOR LUCA:
→ Universal genetic code — almost identical across all life
→ Shared core machinery — DNA polymerase, ribosomes, ATP synthase, key metabolic enzymes
→ Common chirality — all biological amino acids are L-form, all sugars D-form
→ Phylogenetic reconstruction places all known life on a single rooted tree

◆ LUCA was probably:
→ A prokaryote (cell with no nucleus)
→ Living near hydrothermal vents (energy source, mineral substrates)
→ Already had translation, transcription, basic metabolism
→ Before the bacteria/archaea split (which happened relatively early)

💡 WHY IT MATTERS: This is the FINAL synthesis of evolutionary biology. Every concept we've covered — mechanisms (mutation/selection/drift/flow), Hardy-Weinberg, heritability, speciation, deep time, phylogeny — applies because all life shares one lineage. Without LUCA, evolution would just be 'change'; WITH LUCA, evolution is the full historical narrative of every living thing.

🔬 EXAMPLE: When you compare any two species' genomes — humans + corn, E. coli + whales — you find homologous genes from LUCA still doing similar jobs ~3.8 BY later. The universal ribosome is the most conserved structure in biology, recognizable across all 3 domains.

📖 STORY: Darwin closed Origin (1859) with: 'There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one... from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.' Modern phylogenetics confirms — it was indeed ONE form.

💪 TYPICAL EXAM QUESTIONS

[Final-A · MC#10] Earth is approximately how old, based on radiometric dating?
  A. 100 million years
  B. 4.568 billion years
  C. 13.8 billion years
  D. 4.568 million years
→ Answer: B

[Final-A · MC#17] Which of the following best defines biological evolution?
  A. An individual organism becoming better adapted over its lifetime.
  B. Change in the heritable traits of a population across generations.
  C. Progressive improvement of organisms toward greater complexity.
  D. Random variation among individuals within a single generation.
→ Answer: B
